papers.title: A Complementary Dual-Branch Receptive Field Network for Cross-Channel-Density Motor Imagery EEG Decoding.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct communication between the brain and external devices, providing a bio-inspired link between humans and artificial systems. However, electroencephalography (EEG)-based motor imagery (MI) decoding continues to pose challenges, due to limited temporal exploitation and insufficient spatio-temporal modeling. To alleviate these limitations, a complementary dual-branch receptive field network (DBRFNet) is proposed for cross-channel-density MI-EEG decoding. Specifically, two complementary branches with distinct temporal receptive fields are designed to capture multi-scale temporal dynamics. Each branch employs a progressive spatio-temporal module integrating temporal, depthwise spatial, and dilated convolutions for modeling short- and long-range temporal dependencies. The features from the two branches are fused using element-wise addition and further encoded for classification. The proposed method is evaluated on three public datasets representing low-, medium-, and high-density EEG configurations. DBRFNet achieves decoding accuracies of 80.48%, 84.37%, and 92.24% under cross-validation analysis, and 87.76%, 80.94%, and 94.64% under hold-out analysis, demonstrating competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component within the proposed architecture. These results indicate that DBRFNet effectively learns discriminative spatio-temporal representations and provides a robust solution for MI-BCI systems.

papers.title: Psychological Distress and Resources Under Prolonged Exposure to an Environmental Threat: A Qualitative Study on Inhabitants Exposed to the Campi Flegrei's Bradyseism.
papers.abstract: Prolonged environmental threats expose communities to recurring hazard cues and uncertainty, yet psychological consequences and resources involved in adaptation remain underexplored. This study examined psychological outcomes, personal and social resources, and their co-occurrence among inhabitants exposed to bradyseism in Campi Flegrei, southern Italy. Fifty-two semi-structured interviews were conducted with inhabitants of the Campi Flegrei area. Eighteen were recruited without reference to a specific stakeholder role, whereas 34 were recruited based on their institutional, professional, or community roles. Narratives were examined through theory-driven thematic analysis. Six psychological outcomes were considered, including five distress-related negative psychological outcomes (i.e., anxiety, post-traumatic symptoms, depression, sleep disturbances, and suicidal ideation) and one adaptive psychological outcome (i.e., post-traumatic growth). Distress was classified using literature-derived categories, while the Social-psychological Antecedents to Resilience for Adaptation (SARA) classified resources by locus, specificity, and availability. Anxiety-related experiences were most frequent, followed by post-traumatic stress-related experiences, depression-related experiences, and sleep disturbances; post-traumatic growth was rare, and no segments related to suicidal ideation were identified. Risk perception, experience, acceptance, cognitive reappraisal, and place attachment were frequently identified as available resources in narratives involving distress, whereas information emerged predominantly as unavailable and available social support was identified only once in the corpus. These resources co-occurred with manifestations of distress without revealing a consistent protective pattern. The findings document the coexistence of resources and distress without establishing the direction of their relationships or a protective role. Future research should clarify resource-distress directionality and examine whether perceived agency explains why some resource constellations coexist with persistent distress, whereas others are associated with more adaptive responses under prolonged environmental threat.

papers.title: Psychological Inflexibility and Suicidal Ideation in Pregnant Women: A Cross-Sectional Multiple Mediation Analysis of Depressive Symptoms, Insomnia, and Generalized Anxiety.
papers.abstract: Introduction: Suicidal ideation during pregnancy is an important public health concern. Psychological inflexibility may be associated with emotional and sleep-related symptoms linked to suicidal ideation; however, these patterns of association remain insufficiently understood in pregnant women. Objective: The objective was to examine the relationship between psychological inflexibility and suicidal ideation in pregnant women by evaluating the multiple mediating roles of depressive symptoms, insomnia, and generalized anxiety. Method: A quantitative, cross-sectional associative study using latent variables was conducted with 962 pregnant women receiving care at the National Maternal and Perinatal Institute (INMP), located in Cercado de Lima, Lima, Peru, between October and December 2025. Participants completed the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II (AAQ-II), Frequency of Suicidal Ideation Inventory (FSII), Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-2 (GAD-2). Structural equation modeling (SEM) was performed using R version 4.5.1 within the RStudio Version 4.5.1 environment. Results: The proposed model showed a good fit, scaled χ2(179) = 506.334, p < 0.001, robust CFI = 0.968, robust TLI = 0.963, robust RMSEA = 0.052, 90% CI [0.046, 0.057], and SRMR = 0.030. Psychological inflexibility showed a significant direct association with suicidal ideation (β = 0.246, p < 0.001) and significant indirect associations through depressive symptoms (β = 0.245, p < 0.001) and insomnia (β = 0.030, p = 0.007), whereas the indirect association through generalized anxiety was not significant (β = 0.007, p = 0.749). The total indirect association was significant (β = 0.282, p < 0.001), while the direct association remained statistically significant after inclusion of the mediators. Conclusions: Psychological inflexibility was associated with suicidal ideation among pregnant women, with depressive symptoms and insomnia showing significant indirect associations. These cross-sectional findings identify relevant correlates of suicidal ideation that warrant further longitudinal investigation.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture Combined with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia Alleviates Insomnia-Anxiety Comorbidity in Gynecological Cancer Patients Undergoing Chemotherapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Insomnia and anxiety affect many gynecological cancer patients on chemotherapy, and non-pharmacological options are limited. This randomized trial examined whether adding electroacupuncture (EA) to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) improves both conditions. Seventy-six patients received EA + CBT-I or sham EA + CBT-I for 4 weeks. Outcomes included sleep quality (PSQI), insomnia severity (AIS), anxiety (HAMA), objective sleep parameters, and overall response rate. At Week 4, the EA group showed a greater reduction in PSQI global score (mean difference in change from baseline: -3.11, 95% CI: -4.11 to -2.11, p < 0.001). More patients in the EA group achieved AIS ≤ 6 (71.1% vs. 42.1%, p = 0.010) and HAMA ≤ 14 (92.1% vs. 65.8%, p = 0.005). Deep sleep (p = 0.001), REM sleep (p = 0.045), and sleep score (p = 0.008) also increased more with EA group. The overall response rate was higher with EA (92.1% vs. 71.1%, p = 0.016). No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that adding EA to CBT-I improves sleep and anxiety in this population, with a favorable safety profile.

papers.title: Skin-Interfaced Flexible Sensors for Continuous Monitoring of Thermal, Mechanical, Electrical, and Respiratory Signals.
papers.abstract: Skin-interfaced flexible sensors enable physiological monitoring during daily activities, sleep, and rehabilitation, but a sensitive device or a clear waveform does not by itself establish the validity of the physiological information obtained. Many existing reviews emphasize sensor materials, fabrication, device design, and sensing performance. This review instead examines how physiological information is preserved or altered from its origin to its eventual interpretation. We focus on flexible physical sensors for skin temperature, mechanical activity, surface biopotentials, electrodermal activity, and respiration-related monitoring. The scope is restricted to selected physical and skin surface electrical sensing pathways, while optical, biochemical, and implantable technologies are not reviewed in detail. The analysis links the physical quantity available at the skin to its transmission across the skin-device interface, sensor response, signal fidelity, and the physiological output that the measurement can reasonably support. This approach distinguishes direct measurements from derived or clinically interpreted quantities and shows where additional reference-based validation becomes necessary. Across the reviewed modalities, major limitations arise when interface conditions or environmental and mechanical interference alter the relationship between the physiological source and the recorded signal. Reliable monitoring therefore depends on preserving this relationship under intended wearing conditions and demonstrating agreement with references appropriate to the claimed output. By focusing on this measurement process, the review complements materials- and device-oriented surveys and provides a basis for judging flexible sensors according to the physiological information that their measurements can support.

papers.title: Risk and protective factors for posttraumatic stress disorder among Israeli civilians in the aftermath of 7 October: the TERUMAH (Trauma, Civic Engagement, Resilience and Health) study.
papers.abstract: Background: Few studies of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) risk in civilian populations during armed conflict consider a wide range of risk and protective factors.Objective: This study aimed to estimate the population prevalence of PTSD and related risk and protective factors in an Israeli civilian population in the aftermath of 7 October and the subsequent war.Methods: Participants (ages ≥18) completed population-based surveys 6 months after the onset of the 7 October war and again 9 months later (n=813). PTSD was assessed using the PTSD Checklist for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (PCL-5, score>31) among those reporting their most bothersome traumatic event (n=435). Baseline measures included sociodemographics, social wellbeing (social support, social integration, resilience) and coping behaviours (sleep, physical activity, weight gain, smoking/alcohol use, intensity of volunteering). Traumatic exposure and stress included trauma type (direct, indirect and secondary), a count of traumatic experiences, a family member in combat and previous trauma. Multivariable models assessed risk and protective factors for PTSD, adjusting for all covariates.Results: Overall population prevalence of PTSD was 15.6%, and 29.2% among those reporting a traumatic event. Statistically significant risk factors included low vs. high income (13.7% higher predicted probability), high count of traumatic experiences (19.4% higher), worse sleep (11.9% higher) and high perceived threat (12.6% higher). Protective factors included high resilience (14.5% lower predicted probability) and moderate-intensity volunteering (18.5% lower). Sensitivity analyses indicated additional risk/protective factors associated with alternative definitions of PTSD.Conclusion: Findings suggest that among those who experience war-related traumatic events, low income, multiple traumatic events, worsening sleep patterns and high levels of perceived threat may increase risk of PTSD, while moderate levels of volunteering and high levels of resilience may lower that risk. Results suggest volunteering as a novel community-level preventive intervention strategy to reduce the risk of posttraumatic symptoms and PTSD.

papers.title: Antibody-Related Mechanisms in Ocular Diseases: Autoimmunity, Malignancy, and Therapeutic Targeting.
papers.abstract: Antibodies in ocular disease have heterogeneous biological meanings: they may act as direct pathogenic effectors, systemic diagnostic biomarkers, indicators of B-cell clonality, or therapeutic agents. This distinction is particularly important in the eye, where immune privilege and the blood-ocular barrier restrict tissue access, whereas inflammation may permit entry of immunoglobulins, complement, and immune cells or support local humoral responses. This narrative review integrates antibody and B-cell biology across autoimmune and paraneoplastic retinopathies, aquaporin-4-immunoglobulin G-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid, ocular myasthenia gravis, thyroid eye disease, systemic autoimmune and fibroinflammatory disorders with ocular involvement, and B-cell malignancies including vitreoretinal and ocular adnexal lymphoma. We distinguish the evidence for direct antibody pathogenicity from disease association and emphasize that a positive result is interpretable only in relation to the ocular phenotype, assay platform, titer, specimen compartment, and orthogonal confirmation. Serum testing, ocular-fluid analysis, electrophysiology, multimodal imaging, cytology, histopathology, immunophenotyping, immunoglobulin clonality, and molecular testing have complementary roles. Therapeutic strategies include B-cell or B-lineage depletion, complement inhibition, cytokine- or receptor-directed monoclonal antibodies, insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor blockade, and emerging FcRn- or plasma-cell-directed approaches; however, regulatory status and ocular-specific evidence vary substantially among diseases. A mechanistically stratified framework may reduce overdiagnosis, improve recognition of malignant masquerade syndromes, and support more precise selection of targeted therapy.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances and Health-Related Quality of Life in Paediatric Oncology: A Comparative Study with Non-Oncological Chronic Illness and Healthy Peers.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sleep disturbance is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to symptom burden and functioning in paediatric oncology, yet comparative evidence across clinical and healthy populations remains limited. This study examined sleep quality and its association with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents with cancer compared with peers with non-oncological chronic illnesses and healthy controls. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted at Hong Kong Children's Hospital. Participants 6-18 years were recruited by convenience sampling into three groups (oncology, chronic illness, healthy; n = 50 each). Children and adolescents completed the Chinese Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Pediatrics Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0. Group differences were tested using chi-square tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc Tukey comparisons. Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple linear regression examined PSQI-PedsQL associations. Results: Sleep quality differed significantly across groups (p < 0.001), with the poorest sleep observed in the oncology group. The prevalence of poor sleep (PSQI ≥ 5) was 60.0% in oncology group, compared with 40.0% in those with chronic illness and 30.0% in healthy peers. Mean global PSQI scores were 6.02 ± 3.40 in the oncology group, 4.10 ± 2.60 in the chronic illness group, and 3.30 ± 2.35 in healthy controls, with a significant overall group difference (p < 0.001). Impairments were most pronounced in sleep latency, habitual sleep efficiency, and sleep disturbances. HRQoL was lowest in the oncology group (p < 0.001). Mean PedsQL total scores were 68.98 ± 15.73 in the oncology group, 75.99 ± 14.03 in the chronic illness group, and 85.44 ± 10.26 in healthy controls, respectively, with a significant overall group difference (p < 0.001). Across the full sample, poor sleep quality was independently associated with lower HRQoL after adjustment for demographic and clinical factors (β = -0.271, p = 0.002), with no significant interaction by group. Conclusions: Children and adolescents with cancer reported clinically significant sleep impairment, driven mainly by reduced sleep quality and continuity. Routine sleep screening and targeted supportive interventions may improve HRQoL in paediatric oncology.

papers.title: Conductive Polyvinyl Alcohol-Based Hydrogels for Wearable Electronics: Preparation Strategies, Conductivity Enhancement, and Sensing Applications.
papers.abstract: Conductive poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)-based hydrogels combine electrical functionality with the mechanical compliance and biocompatibility required for wearable bioelectronics. However, simultaneously achieving mechanical robustness, stable electrical conductivity, and long-term hydration stability remains challenging. Adopting a performance trade-off perspective focused on wearable sensing, this review examines recent advances in five interconnected areas: (1) fabrication strategies, including freeze-thaw cycling, the Hofmeister effect, mechanical training, and green synthesis routes; (2) conductivity enhancement through electron-conducting pathways (carbon nanofillers, MXene, and conducting polymers), ionic routes (salt and electrolyte doping), and hybrid systems; (3) wearable sensing applications, including physiological monitoring (ECG/EMG/EEG), multimodal biosensing of biofluid analytes, and intelligent sensing devices; (4) environmental resilience and mechanical durability; and (5) regulatory, manufacturing, and clinical translation challenges. Representative studies report tensile strengths exceeding 19 MPa, electrical conductivities above 10 S/m, gauge factors above 10, and self-healing within 1 s; however, these values were obtained for different formulations and under different testing conditions. The review further identifies critical gaps in reproducibility, comparable testing protocols, device-level integration, and scalability, and outlines design considerations for advancing conductive PVA-based hydrogels toward reliable wearable health monitoring systems.

papers.title: Acetaminophen and chronic post-surgical neuropathic pain: a randomized double blind cross-over study.
papers.abstract: Despite not being recommended in treatment algorithms, people often take acetaminophen for pain relief in neuropathic pain. As there is no randomized clinical trial on oral acetaminophen in neuropathic pain, this study aims to evaluate the efficacy of oral therapeutic-dose acetaminophen compared to placebo in patients with peripheral neuropathic pain. This is a randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover, double-blind clinical study. The protocol and informed consent form were approved by the French Research Ethics Committee and National Drug Agency (trial number: NCT03559985). It took place in University Hospital, Clermont-Fd, France. Thirty patients with chronic post-surgery neuropathic pain were randomised. Acetaminophen or placebo was taken for 7 days with a wash-out period of 7 days and treatments were compared. Outcomes were 7-day mean pain intensity (numerical rating scale) after treatment, Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI), Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HAD), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and adverse events. Acetaminophen presents no statistical difference with the placebo for pain report (effect-size [95%CI]: -0.09 [-0.45; 0.26], P = 0.607) and for all secondary outcomes. This study demonstrates no clinically meaningful analgesic benefit of short-term, 3g/day oral acetaminophen as add-on therapy in chronic post-surgical peripheral neuropathic pain, and no adverse events. Although findings should not be generalized, patients with neuropathic pain using self-medicated acetaminophen should always be informed about the risks of long-term use of acetaminophen to avoid unnecessary intake and potential long term adverse events.

papers.title: Systems-level orchestration of oxygenic photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation in cyanobacteria.
papers.abstract: SUMMARYDiazotrophic cyanobacteria represent a unique group of prokaryotes that are capable of performing two physiologically conflicting processes: oxygen-generating photosynthesis and oxygen-sensitive nitrogen fixation. Adaptive evolution over millions of years has culminated in two complex, divergent strategies-spatial and temporal separation-that allow extant cyanobacteria to reconcile these antagonistic pathways. While the long-studied spatial separation strategy utilized by most filamentous strains is well understood at the molecular level, the temporal separation mechanisms in unicellular and non-heterocystous filamentous cyanobacteria remain an expanding but under-reviewed area of research. This review focuses on the orchestration of photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation in cyanobacteria, with an emphasis on temporal separation. We discuss molecular mechanisms driving the synchronization of carbon and nitrogen fixation in filamentous cyanobacteria, highlighting recent findings that elucidate the complex regulatory networks involved in maintaining an optimal C/N balance. In contrast, for unicellular cyanobacteria, where regulatory mechanisms are less defined, we synthesize various discoveries that challenge the prevailing view that these prokaryotes are metabolically disadvantaged by strict diurnal constraints. We review studies that indicate the metabolic plasticity of these strains, potentially conferred by effective oxygen-protective mechanisms, including a robust circadian clock that regulates intracellular oxygen levels. This plasticity allows adaptation to diverse diurnal conditions, preferentially segregating the incompatible processes into opposite phases while also accommodating both processes under light when daylength conditions are suboptimal. Such metabolic flexibility likely predisposes these prokaryotes to be naturally selected for nitrogen-fixing symbioses with eukaryotes and eventually, as recently demonstrated, to evolve into a nitrogen-fixing organelle.

papers.title: Harnessing time: Leveraging chronotype asynchrony to promote efficient speech learning.
papers.abstract: This study examined chronotype synchrony effects on learning a nonnative speech contrast. Fifty-nine young adult native speakers of American English completed a circadian preference questionnaire and trained on producing a Danish vowel contrast in the morning or evening. Perceptual change (discrimination and identification, n = 26) and production change (acoustic distance from a native model, n = 59) were assessed. Identification improved with training, but improvement did not depend on circadian preference or training time. Production gains were greater when training occurred outside learners' preferred time, although the effect was small, suggesting that speech-motor learning may benefit from reduced executive control.

papers.title: Dissociable anterior and posterior beta-burst dynamics track thought disorder in schizophrenia.
papers.abstract: Thought disorder in schizophrenia likely reflects disrupted maintenance of internal models during predictive processing. Beta oscillations have been proposed to index top-down predictive signalling, but prior resting-state studies have focused on spectral power, overlooking transient burst dynamics that potentially stabilize and reinstate internal representations, especially in the default mode network (DMN). Resting-state magnetoencephalography was acquired from 25 patients (7 females) with schizophrenia and 25 matched controls (8 females) between May 2024 and October 2025. Beta bursts (15-30 Hz) were extracted from source-localized cortical time series, and burst rate, duration, power, and inter-regional synchrony were quantified. Associations with computationally derived semantic and syntactic speech features reflecting thought disorder were assessed using principal-component regression in the patient group. Conventional beta power did not differ between groups after correction. In contrast, beta-burst dynamics showed significant group-by-anterior-posterior-position interactions for burst rate (p = 0.018), power (p = 0.0014), and duration (p < 0.001). Within the DMN, patients showed shorter inferior parietal burst duration (t(46.0) = -2.74, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0343) and increased burst synchrony within left prefrontal cortex (t(31.0) = 2.81, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0343) and between prefrontal cortices (t(29.8) = 2.73, FDR-adjusted p = 0.0423). Within the patient group, burst components were associated with speech organization (R2 = 0.47, F(3,19) = 5.66, p = 0.006), driven by the inferior parietal burst-duration component (β = -0.55, p = 0.0036), but did not relate to overall clinical severity. The modest patient sample, short resting-state recording, cross-sectional design, and lack of laminar specificity limit causal and mechanistic inference; burst-speech associations require replication. Schizophrenia is associated with dissociable anterior and posterior beta-burst abnormalities that track objective speech markers of thought disorder. These findings suggest impaired hierarchical coordination of predictive beta signalling as a candidate neurophysiological account linking intrinsic network dysfunction to disorganized thought.

papers.title: Sedation Versus General Anesthesia During Pediatric Electrophysiology Studies: A Paired Comparison.
papers.abstract: Anesthetic strategy may influence tachycardia inducibility during pediatric electrophysiology studies, but direct paired comparisons between sedation and general anesthesia remain limited. This prospective paired-comparison study included 51 pediatric patients aged 5-21 years with supraventricular tachycardia undergoing electrophysiology study under both procedural sedation and general anesthesia during the same session. Procedural sedation consisted of midazolam, fentanyl, and supplemental propofol boluses as needed. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and fentanyl and maintained with sevoflurane. Tachycardia inducibility and electrophysiological parameters were compared between anesthetic conditions using paired analyses. Overall tachycardia inducibility was higher during sedation than during general anesthesia (40/51 [78.4%] vs. 29/51 [56.9%], p = 0.007). No significant differences were observed in atrial effective refractory period, ventricular effective refractory period, atrioventricular nodal Wenckebach point, jump, echo interval, or ventriculoatrial block duration. In patients with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, inducibility decreased from 84.0% during sedation to 60.0% during general anesthesia (p = 0.109). In the Wolff-Parkinson-White/atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia subgroup, inducibility decreased from 73.1% to 53.8% (p = 0.063), and the accessory pathway effective refractory period, measured by extrastimulus pacing, was prolonged under general anesthesia (p = 0.018). Procedural sedation was associated with greater overall tachycardia inducibility than general anesthesia during pediatric electrophysiology studies. The AVNRT and WPW/AVRT subgroups showed numerically lower inducibility under general anesthesia in the same direction as the overall finding, although these subgroup differences did not reach statistical significance. These findings support individualized anesthetic planning that considers the arrhythmia substrate, the need to preserve inducibility for mapping and post-ablation validation, and patient-specific requirements for procedural stability.

papers.title: Music-based interventions for people with kidney failure undergoing haemodialysis.
papers.abstract: People receiving haemodialysis for kidney failure experience substantial symptom burden, including anxiety, depression, and pain, which adversely affect physical function and quality of life. Music-based interventions are increasingly used as non-pharmacological strategies to address these symptoms; however, their effectiveness and the certainty of the evidence remain unclear. An updated systematic review of recent randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is therefore warranted. To assess the effects of music-based interventions on fatigue, blood pressure, depression, pain, anxiety, stress, quality of life, and sleep quality in people with kidney failure receiving haemodialysis. We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and two trials registers up to 16 May 2025. We included RCTs involving participants with kidney failure undergoing haemodialysis, comparing music-based interventions with controls where music-based interventions were not provided (e.g. standard care, headphones without music intervention, or video). We excluded studies involving temporary haemodialysis for acute kidney injury or other conditions. We examined the impact of music-based interventions on fatigue, blood pressure, depression, and pain over the short term (up to four weeks), medium term (four weeks to six months), and long term (more than six months). These outcomes were prespecified as critical outcomes for GRADE assessment and included in the summary of findings table. Other important outcomes included anxiety, sleep quality, stress and quality of life. We used the Cochrane risk of bias 2 tool (RoB 2) to assess bias in the RCTs. We synthesised results for each outcome using meta-analysis, where possible, applying a restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects model. We measured outcomes as mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs when all included studies used the same outcome scale, or standardised mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs when different outcome scales were used. We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence for critical outcomes. We included a total of 27 studies involving 1584 participants, of which 24 studies (1467 participants) contributed to the quantitative synthesis. Comparator interventions included usual care, no intervention, headphones without music or white noise, and video interventions. The studies took place in 13 countries and territories across Asia, Europe, North America, and South America. Critical outcomes Fatigue Music-based interventions may reduce short-term fatigue (measured on the 10-point Piper Fatigue Scale) compared with usual care or other comparator interventions (MD -3.14, 95% CI -3.83 to -2.45; 1 study, 62 participants; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of music-based interventions on medium-term fatigue (SMD -1.99, 95% CI -3.92 to -0.06; I² = 91%; 2 studies, 86 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No studies evaluated fatigue in the long term. Blood pressure The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of music-based interventions on short-term blood pressure (mmHg) (MD -5.95, 95% CI -10.56 to -1.34; I² = 70%; 8 studies, 674 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of music-based interventions on medium-term blood pressure (MD -2.00, 95% CI -14.21 to 10.21; 1 study, 16 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No studies evaluated blood pressure in the long term. Depression The included studies evaluated depression using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Patient Health Questionnaire-9, Beck Depression Inventory and Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Music-based interventions may reduce depressive symptoms compared with usual care or other comparator interventions over the short term (SMD -0.88, 95% CI -1.51 to -0.25; I² = 84%; 6 studies, 489 participants; low-certainty evidence) and medium term (SMD -0.81, 95% CI -1.42 to -0.19; I² = 43%; 5 studies, 203 participants; low-certainty evidence). No studies evaluated depression in the long term. Pain The included studies measured pain using the VAS, Kidney Disease Quality of Life Short Form, and McGill Pain Questionnaire. Music-based interventions may reduce short-term pain compared with usual care or other comparator interventions (SMD -0.89, 95% CI -1.63 to -0.15; I² = 92%; 8 studies, 675 participants; low-certainty evidence). No studies evaluated pain in the medium or long term. Music-based interventions may reduce fatigue, depressive symptoms, and pain in people undergoing haemodialysis in the short term compared with usual care or other comparator interventions. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of music-based interventions on blood pressure in the short term. In the medium term, music-based interventions may reduce depressive symptoms, but the evidence is very uncertain about their effects on fatigue and blood pressure. No studies reported long-term outcomes for these critical outcomes. Further large, well-designed RCTs with longer follow-up are needed to clarify the effects of music-based interventions for this population. papers.title: The Raine Study: a multigenerational Western Australian birth and life-course cohort advancing research on the developmental origins of health and disease.
papers.abstract: The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) framework has transformed understanding of how early-life exposures shape health across the life course, yet populations from Oceania remain underrepresented in this research. The Raine Study is a globally unique, multigenerational longitudinal pregnancy cohort established in Western Australia, one of the world's most geographically isolated regions. The study recruited 2900 pregnant women (Generation1) in 1989, which resulted in 2868 live births forming Generation 2, and is now currently recruiting Generation 3 (the children of Generation 2). This paper describes the evolution of the Raine Study from its origins as a pregnancy cohort grounded in DOHaD to a comprehensive life-course and multigenerational research resource. This resource has led to key research findings that have informed international clinical guidelines and national and state health policies across areas including prenatal development and care safety, neurodevelopment, cardiometabolic health, obesity, liver disease, physical activity, mental health, sedentary behaviour, sleep, and assisted reproductive technologies. Central to the Raine Study's success is a longstanding commitment to participant partnership and engagement, resulting in exceptional retention and strong consumer involvement in governance and research prioritisation. The Raine Study demonstrates the critical value of well-characterised, place-based cohorts for advancing DOHaD and life-course science and provides a globally significant resource to inform prevention strategies, precision medicine, and public health policy across generations.
papers.journal: Journal of developmental origins of health and disease

papers.title: Psychopharmacological advances in neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury.
papers.abstract: Pharmacotherapy is widely used to manage neuropsychiatric sequelae that may interfere with neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI), despite limited TBI-specific evidence. This review summarizes psychopharmacological evidence from the past 18 months and proposes a three-step approach: deprescribing potentially recovery-limiting medications, characterizing individual neuropsychiatric symptoms, and selecting symptom-targeted treatments to support cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and functional recovery after TBI. Methylphenidate shows the most consistent evidence for selected cognitive outcomes, particularly attention and processing speed. Pharmacological approaches to agitation, sleep-wake disorders, depression, fatigue, and posttraumatic headache have been studied, but TBI-specific evidence remains limited or heterogeneous. Sedative, anticholinergic, and cognitive adverse effects, cardiovascular risks, and dependence require consideration in TBI neurorehabilitation. No pharmacological treatment is established as disease-modifying after TBI. Given the limited evidence, psychopharmacotherapy should be individualized, symptom-targeted, and integrated into multidisciplinary TBI neurorehabilitation. Continuous medication review and deprescribing should accompany careful treatment selection and monitoring. Future trials should determine whether symptom improvement translates into better rehabilitation participation, functional independence, and long-term health-related quality of life.

papers.title: Real-world diagnosis and treatment of individuals with migraine in the United States: The Migraine Insights in Diagnosis and Treatment (MIND) study.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to describe the real-world diagnosis and treatment patterns of individuals newly diagnosed with migraine in the United States (US). Over 10% of adults in the US are living with migraine. Recent data from large, population-based studies on the diagnosis and treatment of migraine among individuals in the US who are newly diagnosed with migraine are lacking. The Migraine Insights in Diagnosis and Treatment (MIND) study is a retrospective cohort study conducted using the Optum® Market Clarity database. The study included individuals with a first migraine diagnosis between July 1, 2018, and June 30, 2021 (index date), who were ≥18 years old on the index date, had ≥12 months of pre-index and ≥36 months of post-index continuous claims enrollment, and no diagnosis of migraine or use of migraine-specific medications in the pre-index period. Outcomes included index migraine diagnosis (e.g., migraine type, setting of diagnosis, specialty of the diagnosing healthcare provider [HCP]), and use of medications to treat migraine (e.g., medications indicated for acute treatment, prevention, or both; other analgesics). Medications were further subcategorized into migraine-specific acute (triptans, gepants, ergots, and ditans) and preventive (gepants and calcitonin gene-related peptide [CGRP] targeted monoclonal antibodies [mAbs]) medications. All analyses were descriptive in nature. The study database included 911,128 individuals newly diagnosed with migraine, of whom 154,353 met all study eligibility criteria. Mean age was 46.1 years, 81.1% were female, and 66.3% were commercially insured. Common comorbidities included anxiety (40.5%), depression (28.2%), and sleep disorders (26.9%). The most common HCP specialty for the index migraine diagnosis was primary care (47.0%), followed by neurology (18.0%), and other (15.3%); diagnosis most often occurred in outpatient (89.5%) settings, followed by inpatient (7.7%), and emergency department (2.8%). Only 16.2% of individuals had a diagnostic test within 30 days before or after their index migraine diagnosis. A total of 111,345 (72.1%) individuals filled a prescription for a migraine medication in the 3 years after their index diagnosis, including 94,198 (61.0%) who received a medication for acute treatment and 62,596 (40.6%) who received a medication for prevention. The most commonly used acute migraine medication types prescribed first were NSAIDs (62.8%) and triptans (35.0%), while for prevention, it was beta blockers (23.2%) and anticonvulsants (21.6%). Migraine-specific preventive medications, CGRP-targeted mAbs (8.1%) and gepants (1.2%), were used first less frequently. A total of 71,199 (46.1%) individuals filled a prescription for an opioid in the 3 years after the index diagnosis of migraine, while 19,359 (12.5%) filled a prescription for butalbital. This study highlights the frequent utilization of medications that are not migraine-specific, both for acute treatment and preventive management of migraine. Increased efforts towards education for the optimal management of migraine should be implemented.

papers.title: Continuous Subcutaneous Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Improves Nonmotor Symptoms and Fluctuations in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Nonmotor fluctuations (NMFs) in Parkinson's disease (PD) represent a heterogeneous and disabling feature often linked to pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation from oral levodopa. Continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion (CSFLI) provides 24-h levodopa delivery, with established motor benefits but limited real-world data on NMFs. We investigated changes in motor complications, nonmotor symptoms, and NMFs over 3 months after initiation of CSFLI. In this prospective, single-center, real-world study, 66 patients with advanced PD initiated CSFLI. Longitudinal 3-month data were available for 40 patients. Motor complications were assessed with the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) Part IV, motor severity with UPDRS Part III, and nonmotor symptoms with the Nonmotor Symptom Scale (NMSS); nonmotor fluctuations were evaluated with the Nonmotor Fluctuation Assessment questionnaire (NoMoFa). Additional validated scales assessed sleep, mood, fatigue, autonomic, and behavioral symptoms. Longitudinal changes were analyzed using paired parametric or non-parametric tests, as appropriate, with FDR correction. After 3 months, motor complications significantly improved, with reductions in OFF time and ON time with dyskinesias. Nonmotor symptom burden also improved, with significant reductions in NoMoFa total and NMF-OFF scores, whereas NMF-ON remained unchanged. Improvements were also observed in sleep-related symptoms, depressive symptoms, and quality of life, whereas apathy, autonomic symptoms, and daytime sleepiness did not significantly change. CSFLI was associated with improvements in motor complications and nonmotor fluctuations, particularly OFF-related NMFs, together with benefits in specific nonmotor symptoms. These findings provide preliminary real-world evidence supporting a potential role of CSFLI in the management of NMFs in PD.

papers.title: It is time for idiographic, network-informed clinical research for comorbid insomnia and depression.
papers.journal: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science

papers.title: Cerebellar Continuous Theta Burst Stimulation for Insomnia Disorder: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the effects of cerebellar continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) in insomnia disorder (ID). In this randomized sham-controlled trial, patients with ID received 2 weeks of active or sham cerebellar cTBS. The primary outcome was a ≥ 3-point improvement in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score after treatment. Secondary outcomes included changes in sleep, mood, and resting-state fMRI. Seventy-two patients (51 women; mean age, 44.3 ± 11.6 years) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. More patients in the active than sham group achieved a ≥ 3-point PSQI improvement after treatment (75.0% vs. 33.3%; adjusted OR, 6.06; 95% CI, 2.17-18.50; p < 0.001). Active cTBS reduced PSQI scores versus sham both post-treatment (adjusted mean difference, -3.34; 95% CI, -4.57 to -2.12; p < 0.001) and at 1 month (-3.70; 95% CI, -4.93 to -2.48; p < 0.001), and also improved Insomnia Severity Index, Hamilton Anxiety Scale, and Hamilton Depression Scale at both time points (all p < 0.01). Exploratory fMRI analyses identified several post-treatment connectivity differences between groups, but only right amygdala-right orbitofrontal connectivity showed a significant group-by-time interaction (FDR-adjusted p = 0.038). No serious adverse events occurred. Cerebellar cTBS was well tolerated and promising for ID. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05992285).

papers.title: Bidirectional Interaction Between Clock Genes and Reactive Oxygen Species Production in Carp and Zebrafish Macrophages.
papers.abstract: Our study investigated the bidirectional interaction between circadian clock genes and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in fish monocytes/macrophages (Mo/Mf). Macrophages are key leukocytes whose antimicrobial activity relies on ROS generation. As ROS levels fluctuate across the day and clock genes regulate numerous cellular processes, we examined whether macrophage clock gene activity and ROS production are functionally interconnected. We found that carp Mo/Mf displayed constitutive expression of core clock genes and genes involved in melatonin synthesis and redox balance: Clock genes (per2, clock, cry2, and bmal2) showed rhythmic expression under both light:dark and constant dark conditions and ROS production varied across the day. Ex vivo cell stimulation revealed that immune signals, cortisol, and ROS‑modulating agents altered clock gene expression. Direct ROS donors upregulated multiple clock genes, while inhibition of NADPH oxidase reduced ROS production and changed expression of clock genes. Finally, zebrafish mutants lacking cry1 exhibited changes in ROS production, demonstrating that disruption of the circadian clock affects redox activity. Together, these findings show that carp and zebrafish Mo/Mf possess a functional circadian system and that the ROS and clock pathways influence each other. This interplay may shape daily patterns of immune responsiveness and contribute to time‑dependent variation in host defense.
papers.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Sleep Quality and Sleep Timing in Adolescent Gymnasts: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Given the limited pediatric-specific evidence in this area, we aimed to examine the association between federated-level gymnastics participation and sleep quality and sleep timing in adolescents. The global Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score was defined as the primary outcome, sleep-timing measures as secondary outcomes, and individual PSQI component analyses as exploratory. This observational, cross-sectional comparative study included adolescents aged 12 to 16 years participating in federated gymnastics and controls who did not participate in federated sports. Demographic variables included age, sex, and parental educational level, while training-related variables included weekly training duration, number of training sessions, and training schedule. Sleep quality was assessed using the PSQI, and bedtime, wake-up time, sleep duration, and sleep latency were derived from the corresponding PSQI items. Multiple linear regression models included age, sex, maternal educational level, and paternal educational level as covariates. The study included 60 gymnasts and 37 controls, with baseline differences in age, sex distribution, and parental educational level between groups. Gymnasts trained a median of 12.0 hours/week (Q1-Q3: 8.25 to 20.0) over five sessions/week (Q1-Q3: 4 to 6), with a median training-session end time of 20:30 (range: 18:00 to 22:00). In adjusted analyses, gymnast status was associated with later bedtime (B=0.392 hours, 95% CI 0.043 to 0.740, p=0.028), whereas no statistically significant association was observed between study group and global PSQI score (B=0.311, 95% CI -0.720 to 1.343, p=0.550). Increasing age was associated with later bedtime (B=0.231 hours, p=0.004) and shorter sleep duration (B=-0.398 hours, 95% CI -0.560 to -0.236, p<0.001). Among gymnasts, training-session end time was not associated with global PSQI score (B=0.141, 95% CI -0.344 to 0.625, p=0.563; R²=0.006). Overall, 19/97 participants (19.6%) met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality, although an optimal adolescent-specific clinical cutoff has not been definitively established. No statistically significant difference in adjusted global PSQI score was detected between federated adolescent gymnasts and controls. Gymnast status was associated with later bedtime. Approximately one in five participants met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations, and larger longitudinal studies incorporating objective sleep measures are warranted.

papers.title: Circadian-Based Optimization of Pharmacotherapy in Chronic Diseases: Integrating Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Disease Rhythm.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are endogenous, approximately 24-hour biological cycles that regulate physiological processes, including cardiovascular function, metabolism, immune activity, endocrine signaling, and sleep-wake patterns. These rhythms significantly influence disease pathophysiology and therapeutic responses, making biological time an important determinant of treatment outcomes. Several chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disorders, asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, metabolic syndrome, and psychiatric conditions, exhibit predictable circadian variations in symptom severity and disease activity. Simultaneously, circadian oscillations affect pharmacokinetic processes such as drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, as well as pharmacodynamic mechanisms involving receptor sensitivity and cellular responsiveness. As a result, identical drug doses administered at different times may produce considerable differences in efficacy and toxicity. This review analyzes the role of circadian biology in optimizing pharmacotherapy through the integration of chronopharmacology and chronotherapy. It discusses the molecular basis of circadian regulation and its influence on physiological systems, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. Disease-specific chronotherapeutic applications in cardiovascular, metabolic, endocrine, respiratory, rheumatologic, psychiatric, and oncologic disorders are highlighted. Clinical examples, including evening statin administration, timed bronchodilator use, and modified-release glucocorticoid therapy, highlight the practical benefits of circadian-based therapies. However, evidence remains variable across therapeutic areas, with some chronotherapeutic strategies, such as bedtime antihypertensive dosing, showing conflicting results in recent clinical trials. Further research is needed to define optimal timing recommendations and facilitate wider clinical adoption. Throughout, the strength of evidence is appraised to distinguish chronotherapeutic strategies with sufficient support for routine clinical use from those that remain experimental. The review also discusses emerging developments in chronopharmacokinetic modeling, advanced drug delivery systems, wearable monitoring devices, and precision chronomedicine. Despite promising evidence, broader implementation remains limited by variability in circadian patterns, lack of awareness, and insufficient standardized guidelines. Integrating circadian principles into pharmacotherapy and, ultimately, combining precision chronotherapy with lifestyle-based strategies may offer a promising direction for improving therapeutic precision, disease prevention, and patient outcomes.

papers.title: Assessment of Sleep Quality and Modifiable Disruptors in Postoperative Paediatric Patients: A Clinical Audit.
papers.abstract: Background Sleep disruption is common during postoperative hospitalisation and may be influenced by pain, overnight clinical care, and environmental factors. This quality improvement project assessed sleep quality among postoperative paediatric inpatients and identified potentially modifiable contributors to sleep disturbance. Methodology A clinical audit was conducted on a paediatric inpatient ward between April and June 2026. Children aged 0-18 years admitted following elective or emergency orthopaedic surgery and requiring at least one overnight postoperative stay were eligible. Parents or carers completed a questionnaire after the child's first postoperative night assessing sleep quality, nighttime awakenings, causes of sleep disturbance, ward noise and lighting, clustering of overnight care, assessment of sleep needs, and parent/carer sleep. Responses were analysed descriptively using frequencies and percentages. Results In total, 19 questionnaires were included: 14 from children accommodated in multi-bed bays and five from children in individual cubicles. In bays, eight of 14 (57.1%) children were reported to have fair sleep and six (42.9%) woke more than five times overnight. In cubicles, two of five (40.0%) children were reported to have good sleep and one (20.0%) woke more than five times. Nursing observations were reported as a contributor to sleep disturbance in 10 of 14 (71.4%) children in bays and four of five (80.0%) in cubicles. Pain contributed to sleep disturbance in 10 of 19 (52.6%) children overall. Most respondents reported that the ward was quiet overnight and that lights were kept low. However, only seven of 19 (36.8%) families reported being asked about their child's sleep needs. Parent/carer sleep was also frequently disrupted. Conclusions Postoperative sleep disruption was common, with nursing observations and pain among the most frequently reported contributors. Despite generally favourable perceptions of overnight noise and lighting, opportunities for improvement were identified in assessment of individual sleep needs, coordination of overnight care where clinically appropriate, and optimisation of pain management. A subsequent audit cycle following implementation of these measures will assess their impact on sleep-related outcomes.

papers.title: Effectiveness of a School-Centered Intervention for Myopia and Obesity Comorbidity in Children: A Cluster-Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: The rising comorbidity of myopia and overweight/obesity (OWOB) in children shares modifiable behavioral pathways, yet evidence for integrated prevention remains limited. We conducted a cluster-randomized, hybrid type I effectiveness-implementation trial in 36 pair-matched Beijing schools. Of 4991 enrolled students in Grades 1-4 and 7, 3426 (68.6%) completed the 12-month follow-up. The school-centered "22510SS" intervention targeted outdoor activity, screen time, diet, sleep, and health monitoring. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in spherical equivalent or BMI change, or in the prevalence of myopia, OWOB, or their comorbidity. The intervention improved the overall behavior-improvement rate (39.7% vs. 33.7%; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.00-1.80). In a prespecified analysis, students in Grades 1-4 showed slower myopia progression (OR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.25-0.86); an exploratory analysis suggested benefits among children from less supportive family environments. Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) evaluation showed 100% fidelity for school-based activities, approximately 60% completion of family-facing health-tip dissemination, an incremental cost of ¥215.43 per participant, and a Program Sustainability Assessment Tool (PSAT) score of 6.10/7. The intervention was feasible and improved targeted behaviors but did not produce significant population-level clinical effects within 12 months. Stronger family engagement and longer follow-up may be needed. Trial Registration: NCT05275959.

papers.title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Comprehensive Nursing Care in Improving the Well-Being of Patients With Colon Cancer Who Developed Postoperative Sleep Disorders.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effect of comprehensive nursing care on the psychological state and related indicators of patients with postoperative sleep disorders after colon cancer surgery. We retrospectively selected 121 patients with sleep disorders who underwent colon cancer resection in our hospital between January 2021 and December 2023. After 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM), 52 patients were included in the routine nursing group and 52 in the comprehensive nursing group. Comprehensive nursing care, as documented in medical records, included psychological nursing, pain management, rehabilitation guidance and social support care. Data extracted from medical records and follow-up files showed that the comprehensive nursing group had greater reduction in Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores after surgery than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05); the comprehensive nursing group also had shorter first anal exhaust time, first defecation time and hospitalization duration than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05). The complication incidence rate in the comprehensive nursing group was lower than the routine nursing group, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.080). Improvements in all domains of the Short-Form 36 (SF-36) Health Survey in the comprehensive nursing group were greater than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05). The total score and several component scores of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index decreased more significantly in the comprehensive nursing group (p < 0.05). Comprehensive nursing care is a significant correlated between improved psychological state, rehabilitation-related indicators, quality of life and sleep quality in patients with postoperative sleep disorders after colon cancer surgery.

papers.title: Effects of Psycho-Cardiology Model-Based Psychological and Behavioural Management on Negative Emotions and Sleep Disorders in Patients With Resistant Hypertension Complicated by Anxiety and Depression.
papers.abstract: To explore the effect of psychocardiology model-based psychological and behavioural management on top of routine cardiovascular treatment on negative emotions and sleep disorders in patients with resistant hypertension complicated by anxiety and depression. This retrospective study reviewed electronic medical records and follow-up data of patients treated in the Department of Cardiology of Tonglu Hospital, Hangzhou First People's Hospital Tonglu Campus between August 2022 and May 2025. A total of 126 patients diagnosed with resistant hypertension complicated with anxiety and depression who met the predefined inclusion criteria were enrolled. Based on whether the psycho-cardiology model-related assessment and psychological and behavioural management were systematically documented in their medical records, the patients were divided into a psycho-cardiology group (n = 63) and a regular group (n = 63). Changes in anxiety, depression, sleep quality, and blood pressure level were compared between the two groups during the follow-up period. At the end of follow-up, the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores of the psychocardiology group were significantly lower than those of the regular group (p < 0.05); Reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure were greater in the psycho-cardiology group than in the regular group (p < 0.05). In the long-term management of patients with resistant hypertension and anxiety and depression, the psycho-cardiology model combined with psychological and behavioural management was associated with milder negative emotions, better sleep status, improved autonomic function and more stable blood pressure profiles in this retrospective cohort.

papers.title: Efficacy of Guided Imagery Training in Improving Sleep Quality in Patients With Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Sleep Disorders.
papers.abstract: This work aimed to investigate the effectiveness of guided imagery training in improving sleep quality for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and sleep disorders. This retrospective cohort study utilised propensity score matching (PSM). Patients with stable COPD complicated by sleep disorders, treated at The Affiliated Wuxi People's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University from March 2024 to June 2025, were consecutively identified through a retrospective review of medical records. Sixty patients who underwent guided imagery training combined with standard pharmacotherapy were assigned to the combined treatment group, and 109 patients who received standard pharmacotherapy alone were assigned to the control group. PSM (1:1 nearest neighbour matching without replacement, calliper = 0.02) was applied to balance the two groups, resulting in 53 patients per group for final analysis. The primary outcomes were sleep architecture parameters (e.g., sleep efficiency) and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score. Secondary outcomes included the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score and pulmonary function indicators. Differences in sleep architecture parameters, AIS scores and PSQI scores were compared between the two groups before and after treatment. Before treatment, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of sleep efficiency, sleep latency, number of awakenings, apnoea-hypopnea index (AHI) or minimum oxygen saturation (p > 0.05). After treatment, both groups showed significant improvements, including increased sleep efficiency and minimum oxygen saturation (p < 0.05) and decreased sleep latency, number of awakenings and AHI (p < 0.05), compared with baseline. Post-treatment, the combined treatment group demonstrated significantly higher sleep efficiency and minimum oxygen saturation and significantly lower sleep latency, number of awakenings and AHI than the control group (p < 0.05). Regarding AIS and PSQI scores, no significant intergroup differences were found at baseline (p > 0.05). After treatment, both groups exhibited significant score reductions (p < 0.05), with the combined treatment group achieving significantly lower scores than the control group (p < 0.05). In this retrospective cohort of patients with COPD and sleep disorders, the addition of guided imagery training to the standard pharmacotherapy was associated with significant improvements in subjective and objective sleep quality parameters. This approach may serve as a beneficial adjunctive therapy in this population.

papers.title: A Survey of Anxiety Sensitivity Index Levels in School-Aged Children With Asthma and a Study of Its Influencing Factors and Predictive Models.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the current status of anxiety sensitivity index levels in school-aged children with asthma, explore its influencing factors, establish a risk prediction model, and test its predictive effectiveness. We retrospectively analysed 400 school-aged children with asthma admitted to Yueqing People's Hospital between May 2020 and May 2025. The children were randomly divided into a construction group (n = 280) and a validation group (n = 120) at 7:3 ratio. Based on the anxiety sensitivity index levels, the construction group was further divided into a high-anxiety-sensitive group (n = 65) and a low-to-moderate-anxiety-sensitive group (n = 215); the validation group was similarly divided into a high-anxiety-sensitive group (n = 28) and a low-to-moderate-anxiety-sensitive group (n = 92). Clinical data were recorded. A nomogram prediction model was constructed using the R language software package. The model was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and calibration curves, and validated using the validation groups samples. Multivariate analysis of the construction group showed that the main risk factors for high anxiety sensitivity index in school-aged children with asthma were: primary caregiver education level below high school, asthma control status of partial or uncontrolled, primary caregiver monthly income < CNY 4000, incomplete family situation, and Sleep Disorders Scale for Children (SDSC) score ≥39 (p < 0.05). The predictive model constructed from these factors showed good discrimination ability in internal validation, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.794 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.730-0.858) and a C-index of 0.818 (95% CI: 0.733-0.835). In the validation group, the AUC was 0.799 (95% CI: 0.706-0.892) and a C-index was 0.820 (95% CI: 0.717-0.831), indicating good external predictive power. The main risk factors for high anxiety sensitivity index in school-aged children with asthma are: primary caregiver education level below high school, asthma control status of partial or uncontrolled, primary caregiver monthly income < CNY 4000, incomplete family situation, and an SDSC score ≥39. The nomogram model constructed from these factors can effectively predict the risk of high anxiety sensitivity index in school-aged children with asthma.

papers.title: A Retrospective Study Analysing the Outcomes of Anxiety, Depression, and Sleep Disorders in Post-Chemotherapy Patients With Breast Cancer Based on Symptom-Targeted Supportive Psychological Nursing.
papers.abstract: To analyse the differences in supportive psychological nursing care received by patients with breast cancer during and after chemotherapy. A retrospective cohort study was conducted, selecting 152 patients with breast cancer who received standardised chemotherapy and completed follow-up at our hospital between April 2022 and April 2025. Patients were divided into a supportive care group (n = 76) and a routine care group (n = 76) based on differences in supportive psychological nursing care in their medical records and nursing documentation. The levels of depression, anxiety, psychological distress and sleep quality after chemotherapy were then compared between the two groups. Depression and anxiety levels in the supportive care group were lower than those in the routine care group (p < 0.05). The psychological distress thermometer score and insomnia severity index scores in the supportive care group were significantly lower than those in the routine care group (p < 0.05). Analysis of disease coping strategies showed that patients in the supportive care group scored significantly higher on the coping dimension than those in the routine care group and lower on the avoidance and yielding dimensions (p < 0.05). Supportive psychological nursing care was associated with improved depression and anxiety in patients with breast cancer after chemotherapy.

papers.title: The Association of a Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Nursing Model With Quality of Life in Patients With Chronic Tonsillitis Complicated by Anxiety Disorder: A Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: To examine the association between a mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) nursing model and changes in quality of life in patients with chronic tonsillitis complicated by anxiety disorder. This retrospective study analyzed propensity score-matched data from 110 patients (55 per group) with chronic tonsillitis and comorbid anxiety disorder treated at Yingshang County People's Hospital from February 2023 to October 2025. Based on nursing records, patients received either routine nursing or the MBSR nursing model. Pharyngeal symptom scores, Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scores, Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) scores, Hamilton Anxiety (HAMA) Scale scores, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores, and World Health Organization Quality of Life Brief Version (WHOQOL-BREF) scores were extracted and compared. Polysomnography parameters were also analyzed. Exploratory encephalofluctuogram (EFG) data are presented in the Supplementary Material. Post-nursing, both groups showed significantly lower scores for all eight pharyngeal symptoms and lower GAD-7, HAMA, and PSQI scores and higher MAAS scores compared to pre-nursing values (p < 0.05). The MBSR group demonstrated significantly lower pharyngeal symptom scores, lower GAD-7, HAMA, and PSQI scores, and higher MAAS scores than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05), along with significantly higher scores across all WHOQOL-BREF domains (p < 0.05). Polysomnography revealed significantly shorter sleep latency, fewer microarousals, and a higher proportion of rapid eye movement sleep in the MBSR group (p < 0.05). Exploratory EFG observations are presented in the Supplementary Material. In this retrospective analysis, the MBSR nursing model was associated with lower anxiety levels, higher mindful attention awareness, better sleep quality, and better overall quality of life in patients with chronic tonsillitis complicated by anxiety disorder. Exploratory EFG observations are hypothesis-generating only and require validation with established methods. These findings warrant further investigation in prospective studies.

papers.title: Effects of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Combined With Perioperative Refined Nursing on Postoperative Sleep Disturbances, Anxiety, and Depression in Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
papers.abstract: To assess whether integrating mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) into refined perioperative nursing is associated with improvements in postoperative sleep disturbances, anxiety, and depression in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We retrospectively reviewed 146 CABG patients treated at Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, from July 2023 to August 2025. To reduce selection bias, 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) was performed based on baseline characteristics, yielding 73 matched pairs for analysis. Based on the nursing protocol documented in the medical records, patients were classified into two groups: a standard care group had received standard refined perioperative nursing, while an MBSR group had received the same care supplemented with MBSR. Outcome measures included Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) scores assessed preoperatively and on postoperative day 7, objective sleep architecture indices obtained via actigraphy on the day of surgery and on postoperative day 7, length of hospital stay, time to first postoperative ambulation, incidence of sleep disturbances on postoperative day 7, and serum levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6), cortisol, orexin, and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) measured preoperatively and at 24 and 72 hours postoperatively. Statistical analyses included t-tests, repeated measures analysis of variance, and chi‑square tests. After PSM, 73 patients were included in each group, with all standardized mean differences <0.1. Baseline preoperative HADS scores did not differ between groups (p > 0.05). On postoperative day 7, bothgroups showed reductions in (HADS-Anxiety) HADS-A and HADS-Depression (HADS-D), with the MBSR group exhibiting significantly lower scores on all HADS subscales than the standard care group (p < 0.05). PSQI scores on the day of surgery were similar (p > 0.05); On postoperative day 7, both groups improved in total PSQI and across its seven domains versus the surgical day. The MBSR group had significantly better scores than the standard care group for all PSQI domains and total score except subjective sleep quality and hypnotic use(p < 0.05). Time to first postoperative ambulation was shorter and the rate of sleep disturbance on postoperative day 7 was lower in the MBSR group (p < 0.05); mean hospital stay did not differ (p > 0.05). Objective sleep parameters on the day of surgery were comparable (p > 0.05); on postoperative day 7 both groups showed increased total sleep time and sleep efficiency, with greater gains in the MBSR group (p < 0.05). Nighttime awakenings decreased in both groups, with the MBSR group showing a larger reduction (p < 0.05). Repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed significant effects of time, group, and time-by-group interaction for cortisol, orexin, IL-6, and TNF-α (p < 0.05). Within-group analyses showed postoperative increases in cortisol, IL-6, and TNF-α at 24 and 72 hours and declines in orexin versus baseline (p < 0.05). Between-group comparisons at 24 and 72 hours postoperatively demonstrated lower cortisol, IL-6, and TNF-α and higher orexin in the MBSR group compared with the standard care group (p < 0.05), and the temporal patterns differed significantly between groups (p < 0.05). Refined perioperative nursing incorporating MBSR was associated with alleviation of negative emotions in patients undergoing CABG, a lower incidence of sleep disturbances on the 7th postoperative day, and shorter time to first postoperative ambulation.

papers.title: Relationship Between Psychiatric Drug Use and Cognitive Function in Women During the Menopausal Transition: An Analysis Based on the NHANES Database.
papers.abstract: Women during the menopausal transition often experience mood disorders, sleep disturbances, and cognitive decline, making the use of psychotropic drugs relatively common. However, the relationship between psychiatric drug use and cognitive function in menopausal women remains unclear. This was a cross-sectional study that included women aged 45-65 years from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2021-2023 cycle. Psychiatric drug use was defined based on prescription drug data, including antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and sedative-hypnotics. Cognitive function was assessed using the Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST). The Bayesian Kernel Machine Regression model was used to analyse the relationship between psychiatric drug use and cognitive function, with adjustment for potential confounders, including routine demographic characteristics. A total of 956 women during the menopausal transition were included in the analysis. As the number of psychotropic drugs used increased, cognitive function decline became more pronounced. Antidepressants and benzodiazepines played dominant roles in this association (posterior inclusion probability >0.9). The concurrent use of two or more psychotropic drugs was associated with an 11%-24% reduction in DSST cognitive scores. In the context of three-drug combinations, the cognitive impairment associated with antidepressants and benzodiazepines were amplified, resulting in an additional 5.1%-6.3% decrease in cognitive scores. Psychiatric medication use showed a significant cross-sectional association with poorer cognitive performance among women undergoing menopausal transition, and polypharmacy regimens displayed stronger associations than single-drug regimens. Clinically, greater attention should be paid to the potential cognitive impact of psychiatric drug use in menopausal women, and polypharmacy regimens should be optimised.

papers.title: Coping-Strategies as a Mediator Between Symptoms of Sleeping Problems and Risk of Suicide.
papers.abstract: Suicide is a complex, global phenomenon linked to various intersecting vulnerability factors. Among these, sleep-related symptoms represent a significant yet understudied contributor to suicide risk. This study explored whether the concurrent relationship between sleep-related symptoms and suicide risk is statistically mediated by distinct coping strategies within an exploratory cross-sectional framework, addressing data non-normality through robust analytical methods. A total of 1014 participants (33.83% male, 66.17% female) aged 18 to 75 years (M = 33.00, SD = 15.15) participated in an online survey distributed through snowball recruitment. Participants completed the amplified Sleep Symptom Subscale (Su-a) of the Brief Symptom Checklist (LSB-50), the Coping with Stress Questionnaire (CSQ), and the Risk of Suicide Scale (RS). Multiple mediation analyses were conducted to evaluate the indirect effects of coping dimensions while adjusting for sex, age, educational attainment, and socioeconomic status. Sleep-related symptoms were positively associated with suicide risk. Negative self-focus emerged as the strongest mediator (β = 0.112, 95% CI [0.083, 0.143]), whereas Positive Reappraisal (β = 0.018, 95% CI [0.007, 0.032]) and Seeking Social Support (β = 0.012, 95% CI [0.001, 0.024]) acted as protective mediators. Overt emotional expression also showed a small but significant indirect effect (β = 0.009, 95% CI [0.001, 0.018]). A significant direct effect of sleep-related symptoms on suicide risk remained, indicating partial mediation. The findings suggest that coping processes contribute to the connection between sleep difficulties and suicide risk. Interventions aimed at reducing maladaptive coping and strengthening adaptive coping skills may help diminish suicidal vulnerability among individuals experiencing sleep disturbances.

papers.title: Bipolar Disorder and Epilepsy: Clinical and Neurobiological Overlaps, Evidence Gaps, and an Exploratory Systems Perspective.
papers.abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests that bipolar disorder (BD) and epilepsy share important clinical, neurobiological, and therapeutic features. Both disorders are characterized by recurrent episodes and fluctuating clinical courses, raising the possibility that partially overlapping or analogous regulatory processes may contribute to some aspects of their clinical expression and progression. This review examines current evidence regarding the overlap between BD and epilepsy and explores integrative perspectives that may help explain their similarities. A narrative review of the literature was conducted. Evidence related to genetics, neuroimaging, cognition, neuroplasticity, neuroinflammation, stress biology, network neuroscience, and treatment response was examined. Findings across BD and epilepsy reveal partially overlapping biological and clinical features, including alterations in excitation-inhibition balance, neuromodulatory disturbances, neuroinflammatory processes, and neuroplastic changes. Neuroimaging studies in both conditions reveal abnormalities in large-scale brain networks involved in emotional regulation, cognitive control, and behavioral adaptation. Clinically, both disorders show sensitivity to environmental and physiological stressors and sleep disruption, cognitive impairment, and partial responsiveness to overlapping pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions. These observations are compatible with the hypothesis that recurrent episodes and prolonged network dysregulation may reinforce maladaptive patterns of instability through interacting feedback processes, although this interpretation remains to be tested directly. Current evidence identifies several clinical and biological similarities between BD and epilepsy but does not yet establish that these similarities reflect identical or directly shared causal mechanisms. An integrative perspective combining network dysfunction, neuroplasticity, and systemic regulatory processes may provide a useful heuristic framework for investigating disease heterogeneity, progression, and treatment response. Further longitudinal and comparative studies are required before this perspective can support personalized monitoring strategies or mechanism-informed interventions.

papers.title: Longitudinal associations between appearance-related social media consciousness and sleep in U.S. middle schoolers.
papers.abstract: Social media use has been linked to poorer sleep outcomes in adolescents, yet the mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. Appearance-related social media consciousness (ASMC)-a preoccupation with one's appearance online-could relate to offline behaviors, including sleep. This study examined the association between ASMC and various sleep behaviors using a parallel mediation structural equation model. Participants were 1158 U.S. 8th-grade students (Mage = 13.14, 52% girls, 36% Hispanic/Latine, 37% qualified for free or reduced-price lunch) surveyed at two points across an academic year. Higher ASMC was indirectly associated with poorer sleep quality, increased sleep disturbances, and longer sleep onset latency through greater compulsive nighttime social media use. Additionally, higher ASMC was indirectly associated with earlier sleep onset times through longer morning routine durations.
