Findings suggest that appearance-related experiences on social media have implications for adolescent sleep health and provide preliminary support for some pathways through which its effects may occur.
papers.journal: Journal of research on adolescence : the official journal of the Society for Research on Adolescence

papers.title: Four weeks of isometric handgrip training results in lower awake ambulatory blood pressure compared with control: a randomized clinical trial.
papers.abstract: We compared the effects of upper-limb (handgrip) and lower-limb (knee extension) isometric training on ambulatory blood pressure in individuals with controlled hypertension. In this randomized controlled trial, 67 adults receiving antihypertensive medication were allocated to a control group (CG, n = 22), small muscle mass isometric training (SMM, handgrip; n = 22), or large muscle mass isometric training (LMM, knee extension; n = 23). Participants completed 12 supervised sessions over 4 weeks, with the exercise protocols performed at 30% of upper-limb MVC or lower-limb maximal isometric load, respectively. Ambulatory blood pressure outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline office blood pressure. Hourly 24-h profiles were analyzed using generalized estimating equations with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc tests. Significant between-group differences were observed only for awake ambulatory blood pressure. Compared with CG, SMM showed lower awake systolic blood pressure (121.8 ± 3.1 vs. 124.2 ± 2.6 mmHg; p = 0.017) and awake diastolic blood pressure (76.3 ± 3.6 vs. 80.8 ± 4.2 mmHg; p = 0.009). No significant differences were observed between LMM and CG, between the two exercise groups, or for 24-h and sleep blood pressure. These findings indicate that, after 4 weeks of supervised isometric training, modest between-group differences in awake ambulatory blood pressure were observed only for handgrip training compared with the control group. Greater muscle mass recruitment did not result in superior antihypertensive effects, suggesting that the chronic blood pressure response to isometric exercise is not determined solely by the amount of muscle mass involved. Trial registration: "ClinicalTrials.gov," "NCT07147595."

papers.title: Epigenetics in Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.abstract: Following traumatic brain injury (TBI), changes in proteins, metabolites, and gene expression are highly dynamic and are influenced by genetic and environmental factors, circadian rhythms, and injury characteristics, including injury type (focal or diffuse), severity (mild to severe), and stage of recovery (acute, subacute, and chronic). These molecular alterations are accompanied by epigenetic modifications that regulate gene expression and contribute to injury progression and recovery. In this review, we integrate and summarize preclinical and clinical studies examining DNA methylation, histone methylation and acetylation, microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulation, RNA epigenetic modifications, and mitochondrial epigenetic (mitoepigenetic) changes following TBI. Most studies have focused on DNA methylation, histone modifications, and miRNAs in experimental models, providing important insights into cell type-specific epigenetic responses after injury. We also review studies evaluating therapeutic strategies, including DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase inhibitors, that target epigenetic mechanisms to improve TBI outcomes.

papers.title: How Nurses Assess Interventions to Promote Patients Sleep on Hospital Wards: Results of a Self-Report Survey.
papers.abstract: The aim of this study is to describe how nurses assess interventions to promote patients' sleep on hospital wards. The study was a cross-sectional survey, and it was conducted among nurses in Finnish specialist healthcare in 2022. Out of 482 eligible participants in the sampling frame, 129 nurses returned a completed questionnaire. The open-ended question was answered by 36 participants. Data were analysed using statistical methods and inductive content analysis. In general, participants assessed that they perform well in sleep-promoting activities in a hospital ward. Participants gave the highest assessment to supporting patients' mental and emotional well-being. Minimising disturbance related to nursing interventions got the lowest scores. Based on the open-ended questions, respondents described that the realisation of patients' sleep support in the hospital related to the care environment, patient placement within the ward, resources available for nursing interventions, sleep-supporting aids, care culture and training related to supporting patients' sleep. Nurses assess that they are implementing patient sleep-promotion interventions well. Nurses realise patients' sleep promotion as a part of their daily activities. Nurses can promote patient's sleep with small activities, as long as the organisation takes care of the nurses' skills and ensures practical interventions so that the patient gets enough rest during the treatment period.

papers.title: Sleep Duration Phenotypes and Dynamic Homeostasis: A Wave-Model Framework.
papers.abstract: Are sleep duration and sleep intensity manifestations of the same phenotype, or are they distinct, complementary traits? We addressed this question by removing two major constraints on phenotype expression: limited sleep opportunity and prior sleep deficit. Across 105 baseline 8-h nights and 420 extended 14-h nights in 15 individuals, sleep duration and NREM intensity behaved as two largely independent traits. Baseline expression of each parameter predicted its own subsequent expression during chronic sleep abundance but failed to predict the companion trait either within or between conditions. We then evaluated external evidence from chronic 4- and 6-h sleep restriction alongside extreme natural sleep-duration phenotypes, interpreting these findings through the wave model of sleep dynamics. In this framework, sleep duration reflects the geometry of sleep-cycle oscillations, determined primarily by the width of the sleep-state stability landscape (formally represented as a Morse potential well). Conversely, NREM intensity reflects oscillation amplitude, providing a visible signature of deviation from homeostatic equilibrium. While acute perturbation alters amplitude, chronic perturbation induces adaptive changes in landscape width, preserving a characteristic deviation from equilibrium despite severe shifts in underlying state instability and allostatic strain.

papers.title: Why sleep assessment belongs in the memory clinic.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent in older adults and are particularly common among individuals attending memory clinics for assessment of cognitive impairment. Emerging evidence links sleep disorders, including insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, circadian rhythm disruption, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, to cognitive decline, neurodegenerative pathology, and reduced quality of life for patients and caregivers. Despite their high prevalence and clinical relevance, sleep disturbances are not routinely assessed within many memory clinic and neurologic, psychiatric, and geriatric settings, and approaches to screening, diagnosis, and management vary widely across health-care systems. This Perspective article examines current approaches to sleep assessment and management within memory clinic and specialized settings across four international contexts. We highlight the absence of systematic approaches to identifying and managing sleep disturbances in this population and propose the need for a pragmatic stepped-care framework to improve detection, guide referral pathways, and support more consistent and personalized care in memory clinic settings.
papers.journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

papers.title: Indirect moxibustion therapy improves insomnia and associated symptoms in patients with schizophrenia.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of low-dose dexzopiclone combined with Indirect moxibustion (IM), compared with sham Indirect moxibustion (SIM), on sleep quality (PSQI) and quality of life (SQLS) in patients with schizophrenia and comorbid insomnia. This single-center randomized controlled trial (NCT06171308) obtained ethics approval from Shanghai Mental Health Center (SMHC-IRB-2023-08). A total of 120 participants were randomly assigned to the IM group (n = 60) or the SIM group (n = 60), receiving 8 weeks of standardized intervention. Baseline PSQI and SQLS scores were comparable between the two groups. After 4 and 8 weeks, the IM group demonstrated significantly lower PSQI and SQLS scores than the SIM group (PSQI at week 4: 10.10 ± 1.76 vs. 13.50 ± 1.65, week 8: 10.65 ± 1.54 vs. 12.77 ± 2.05, SQLS at week 4: 28.78 ± 8.84 vs. 35.56 ± 3.38, week 8: 30.36 ± 10.63 vs. 38.07 ± 3.42). The improvement in the IM group was significantly greater than that in the SIM group in terms of change from baseline (PSQI: -3.399 [95% CI: -4.078 to -2.719] at week 4, -2.115 [95% CI: -2.795 to -1.435] at week 8, SQLS: -6.801 [95% CI: -9.104 to -4.462] at week 4, -7.732 [95% CI: -10.071 to -5.393] at week 8), with all adjusted intergroup differences being statistically significant (P < 0.001). Adjunctive Indirect Moxibustion led to statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in sleep quality and quality of life compared to sham procedure in this patient population over an 8-week period. These preliminary findings suggest IM is a promising adjunctive therapy. Further multicenter, long-term trials with expanded outcome indicators are required to validate its generalizability and sustained efficacy.

papers.title: Bridging the gap: advanced chromatin biotechnologies for circadian epigenomic profiling in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
papers.abstract: Surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy remain the main therapies for treating head and neck cancers, however new modalities have emerged with an emphasis to understand the complexity of the tumor biology. One emerging layer of complexity is the circadian clock, disrupted in many cancers, contributes to pathogenesis and progression due to its crosstalk with cancer pathways. While transcriptional alterations of core clock genes have been described in Head and Neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), the higher-order epigenetic and chromatin-based mechanisms underlying circadian dysregulation remain poorly defined. In this review, we highlight the potential of several chromatin-based biotechnologies in characterizing circadian clock disruption and identifying epigenetic biomarkers in HNSCC. Powerful assays including Chromatin conformation capture, Chromatin immunoprecipitation, DNA methylation profiling, ATAC-seq and single cell technologies can dissect circadian disruption at multiple regulatory layers. These approaches enable genome-wide mapping of chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and 3D chromatin organization. Integrating these approaches across HPV-positive (HPV+) and HPV-negative (HPV-) HNSCC provides a framework to determine whether circadian disruption reflects transcriptional deregulation alone or involved structural genome remodeling that actively drives tumor progression. Linking circadian disruption to epigenomic reprogramming in HNSCCs can serve to identify mechanisms of therapeutic resistance and identify vulnerabilities. Advancing chromatin-informed circadian biomarker discovery in HNSCC has the potential to shift precision oncology from static genomic profiling toward dynamic, architecture-based epigenetic regulation.

papers.title: Respiratory health risks associated with humidifier disinfectant exposure in South Korea: A systematic review and meta-analysis with exposure-response evaluation.
papers.abstract: Humidifier disinfectants (HDs) were used as household biocidal products to prevent microbial growth in humidifiers and were withdrawn from the South Korean market in 2011 following recognition of associated health risks. Although epidemiological studies have reported associations between HD exposure and various respiratory diseases, the overall strength of evidence and exposure-response relationships have not been comprehensively quantified. This study aimed to systematically review and quantitatively synthesize observational studies to evaluate the association between HD exposure and respiratory diseases and to assess exposure-response relationships across multiple exposure metrics. PubMed, Excerpta Medica Database, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature were searched through September 19, 2025. The primary outcome was the pooled odds ratio (OR) for respiratory disease risk among exposed versus non-exposed individuals. Secondary outcomes assessed exposure-response relationships using categorical and continuous exposure metrics. Seventeen observational studies conducted in South Korea were included. HD exposure was associated with a markedly increased risk of respiratory diseases (pooled OR 7.02, 95% CI 1.97-24.98), with the strongest association observed for lung injury (pooled OR 94.53, 95% CI 61.31-145.73). Age-stratified subgroup analyses exhibited significantly elevated risks across adult, pediatric, and mixed-age populations. Exposure-response analyses demonstrated significant associations across multiple categorical exposure metrics, including usage duration, daily usage hours, cumulative use hours, airborne concentration, cumulative exposure level, longer use during sleep, and HD use during sleep. Continuous exposure analyses indicated that affected individuals had significantly longer cumulative use hours than unaffected individuals (pooled standardized mean difference 0.197, 95% CI 0.069-0.325). This study provides quantitative evidence supporting strong associations between HD exposure and respiratory diseases and demonstrates consistent exposure-response relationships across multiple exposure metrics, supporting a causal relationship between inhalational exposure to HDs and adverse respiratory outcomes. This study provides comprehensive quantitative evidence that humidifier disinfectant exposure is strongly associated with respiratory diseases and demonstrates consistent exposure-response relationships across multiple exposure metrics. These findings strengthen causal inference for inhalational toxicity of humidifier disinfectants and highlight the importance of exposure assessment in environmental health risk evaluation. The results provide important evidence for environmental health policy, risk assessment, and prevention strategies for inhalation exposure to household biocidal products.
papers.journal: Journal of exposure science & environmental epidemiology

papers.title: Workplace and personal predictors of well-being in the broader maternity and neonatal workforce during COVID-19: evidence from a multicentre survey.
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic placed unprecedented pressures on maternity and neonatal services, disrupting models of care and amplifying existing stressors for healthcare staff. While much of the literature has focused on doctors and midwives, less is known about the emotional well-being of the broader multidisciplinary maternity and neonatal workforce, including neonatal nurses, sonographers, allied health, and administrative staff. Understanding the collective impact of workplace and personal factors on emotional well-being across this multidisciplinary group is essential for developing effective, inclusive workforce support strategies. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among maternity and neonatal staff, including doctors, midwives, nurses, sonographers, allied health, and administrative staff, from one tertiary and two secondary Australian hospitals. Survey responses were analysed using exploratory factor analysis to identify subscales representing key dimensions of emotional well-being, as well as workplace-related and personal factors influencing it. These subscales were then used in multiple hierarchical regression analyses to determine predictors of emotional well-being among staff. The strongest predictor of emotional well-being was the subscale 'Impact of COVID-19 on the Workplace' (β = -0.345, p < 0.001), encompassing factors such as perceived risk of contracting COVID-19, staff ability to perform duties, and adverse patient outcomes. Other significant predictors included average sleep duration (β = -0.230, p < 0.001), substance use (β = -0.210, p < 0.001), and time spent on outdoor activities (β = -0.130, p < 0.001). The predictive model explained 35.1% of the variance in emotional well-being (R² = 0.351). Workplace-related and personal factors significantly influenced maternity and neonatal staff well-being during the pandemic. Addressing workplace stress, promoting sleep, supporting healthy coping mechanisms, and encouraging restorative activities may improve staff well-being. These findings can inform the design of targeted workforce support programs and guide service planning strategies to strengthen resilience during future system shocks. Not applicable.

papers.title: As Natural as Sleep: A Literature Study of Catholic Perspectives on Palliative Sedation.
papers.abstract: The Roman Catholic Church has a long-standing tradition of participating in the debates on the ethics of medical care. At the heart of the Church's reflections on this subject lies a deep respect for the dignity of individual patients and human life in general. This respect is also an expression of reverence for God and an acknowledgement of His sovereignty over human life. In the context of palliative care, these basic convictions have led to a strong rejection within Catholicism of those treatments that actively seek to end a patient's life (e.g. euthanasia, medical assistance in dying). Catholic views on palliative sedation, another possible end-of-life treatment, are less clear and forthright. As religion influences the attitudes of both patients and healthcare professionals towards end-of-life treatments, it is important to know and understand these views. This study aims to answer the following research question: what are the perspectives on palliative sedation within the catholic tradition? A comprehensive, systematic literature study was conducted, to identify and map the different perspectives on palliative sedation within the Catholic tradition. The methodology of a scoping review was adopted. The analysis of the sources was based on the Grounded Theory model and the model of systematic reviewing argument-based literature. This study draws on a wide range of sources, both academic and non-academic. The initial conclusion is that palliative sedation is welcomed as a means of alleviating patients' suffering. However, there are reservations. One such concern is that palliative sedation should be clearly distinguished from deliberate efforts to end the life of the patient. There are also concerns about the effect that the impaired consciousness could have on patients' spiritual lives.

papers.title: Substituting Hydromorphone for Morphine in Medical Aid in Dying: Clinical and Practice Implications.
papers.abstract: A morphine shortage in 2024-2025 led Medical Aid in Dying (MAiD) prescribers to substitute hydromorphone for morphine. To evaluate associations between substitution and time to death and sleep among patients supported by Denver Health's MAiD program, which serves Colorado. Quasi-experimental pre-post study of patients between January 2024 and February 2026 with verified ingestion, time to sleep, and time to death. Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models compared time to death and sleep. Among 83 patients, median time to death did not differ between hydromorphone and morphine (55 vs. 65.5 minutes; p = 0.29). Median time to sleep was shorter with hydromorphone (3 vs. 5.5 minutes; p = 0.0007). After adjusting for age, hydromorphone was associated with a twofold faster time to sleep (adjusted hazard ratio 2.08, 95% CI: 1.29-3.36). Hydromorphone was associated with shorter time to sleep than morphine, with no significant difference in time to death. Further study should assess its use as an alternative to morphine.

papers.title: Treadmill or Overground? Cognitive-Motor Interference Effects in Healthy Older Individuals.
papers.abstract: Walking is increasingly understood as a cognitively demanding activity requiring the integration of sensory processing, motor control and executive functions. When combined with a concurrent cognitive task (dual-tasking), cognitive-motor interactions may lead to changes in gait, behaviour and neurophysiology. In healthy aging, reduced motor automaticity may result in greater involvement of top-down control, increasing susceptibility to cognitive-motor interference and fall risk, even in the absence of clinical impairment. To explore real-world demands, we compared dual-tasking during outdoor overground walking and during indoor treadmill walking, using behavioural assessment of cognitive task performance, mobile electroencephalography and motion tracking with wearable sensors. Thirty-six older adults performed an auditory Go/No-Go task during both walking conditions and in a seated control condition. Compared to a stationary control condition, results confirmed significant dual-task interference effects during both walking conditions, and this effect was more pronounced during overground walking. The results suggest that overground walking imposes greater demands, leading to increased competition between cognitive and motor processes for shared cognitive resources. The consideration of natural conditions helps to identify the cognitive demands of locomotion.

papers.title: Sleep and Awake Bruxism and Mental Health Conditions: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of the 1982 Pelotas Birth Cohort.
papers.abstract: To investigate the long-term prevalence of self-reported sleep bruxism (SB) and awake bruxism (AB) and their association with mental disorders in adults from the 1982 Pelotas Birth Cohort, Southern Brazil. Data on SB and AB were collected at age 40 using subject-based reports. Symptoms of common mental disorders (CMD) were assessed using the Self-Reporting Questionnaire (SRQ-20) at ages 30 and 40, and specific mental disorders were assessed using the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (M.I.N.I.) at age 40. Exploratory variables included demographics, socioeconomic status, mental health history, and unhealthy behaviors. Associations were analyzed using crude and adjusted Poisson regression models with robust variance. Both were associated with female sex (PR 1.48, 95% CI 1.27-1.72 for AB; PR 1.47, 95% CI 1.27-1.70 for SB) and alcohol dependence (PR 1.47, 95% CI 1.09-1.99 for AB; PR 1.34, 95% CI 1.00-1.79 for SB). Depression was associated with a higher prevalence of AB (PR 1.50, 95% CI 1.10-2.05) and SB (PR 1.41, 95% CI 1.05-1.90). Participants who experienced probable CMD at both 30 and 40 years had a higher prevalence of AB (PR 2.02, 95% CI 1.62-2.52) and SB (PR 1.52, 95% CI 1.23-1.88) compared with those who had never experienced probable CMD. Patterns of probable common mental disorders were associated with a higher prevalence of self-reported SB and AB at age 40.

papers.title: Erebosis: An Emerging Concept of a New Type of Regulated Cell Death.
papers.abstract: This review briefly describes the discovery of a morphologically distinct form of regulated cell death in Drosophila, termed erebosis, which is characterized by organelle loss, nuclear flattening, and intracellular accumulation of Ance. The latter serves as a biomarker of this type of cell death but does not act as its trigger. Erebosis can be induced by amino acid deprivation accompanied by the reduced cytoplasmic viscosity, and its development is also associated with the increased heme oxygenase activity and decreased intracellular heme levels. We hypothesize that the heme-sensing protein E75 in Drosophila melanogaster, a homolog of mammalian REV-ERB proteins involved in circadian regulation, may provide a link between erebosis and renewal of enterocytes from the intestinal stem cells. Finally, we discuss the differences between erebosis and other forms of regulated cell death, as well as detection of ACE2 in the brains of mice in different models of Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Clinical feature-guided targeted genetic testing in early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy: a real-world diagnostic approach in a resource-limited setting.
papers.abstract: In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), access to trio-based whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing is limited, which may delay genetic diagnosis in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE). We used clinical features to guide targeted genetic testing and reviewed the results through multidisciplinary discussion in a Vietnamese pediatric cohort with early-onset DEE and examined its association with treatment decision-making. We prospectively enrolled 51 children aged 0-23 months with early-onset DEE at a tertiary pediatric center in Vietnam between November 2023 and April 2025. Clinical phenotyping included seizure semiology, EEG, and brain MRI. Prior to testing, patients were categorized as hypothesis-driven or non-hypothesis-driven based on clinical and paraclinical features. Targeted sequencing of 108 DEE-associated genes was performed. Variants were reviewed by geneticists and then discussed in multidisciplinary sessions including clinicians. Treatment changes and seizure outcomes were assessed six months after genetic results were disclosed. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in 25 of 51 patients (49%). Diagnostic yield differed between the hypothesis- driven and non-hypothesis-driven groups (93.3% vs 30.6%, p < 0.001). Channelopathy-related genes accounted for the largest proportion of genetic diagnoses. Among genetically diagnosed patients, 20 of 25 had a treatment change accompanied by a ≥ 50% reduction in seizure frequency. In genotype-negative patients with infantile spasms syndrome, phenotype-guided treatment adjustment was followed by effective seizure control in most cases. In this cohort, using clinical features to guide targeted genetic testing, combined with multidisciplinary review of results, was associated with higher diagnostic yield in a hypothesis-driven subgroup and was frequently accompanied by treatment changes linked to improved seizure control.

papers.title: Revealing contour integration-related ERPs through temporal separation from early visual evoked potentials.
papers.abstract: Contour integration has been proposed to involve coordinated processing across hierarchical cortical regions. Previous ERP studies have focused primarily on time windows around 200 ms post-contour onset, identifying the occipital N200 and N2pc, which are primarily responsible for visual awareness of integrated shapes and its reliance on spatial attention, respectively. However, findings regarding ERPs at earlier and later stages, as well as how contour properties modulate ERPs related to contour integration, remain unclear. This gap largely stems from traditional paradigms presenting contours at trial onset, confounding early visual evocation with contour integration. To resolve this, we employed a paradigm that temporally dissociates the two processes. By varying contour fidelity, we identified two additional components alongside the occipital N200 and N2pc: an early effect (~100 ms) reflecting feature binding and a late P3b component reflecting task-related effort. Furthermore, the occipital N200 was differentially modulated by contour fidelity and detectability: reducing fidelity through misalignment of contour components decreased its amplitude without affecting latency, whereas reducing detectability through oblique orientation increased latency without affecting amplitude. These findings suggest that the occipital N200 reflects recurrent shape processing, a crucial step in which attended, bound features are integrated into a coherent visual representation that enters conscious awareness, shedding light on how hierarchical processes cooperate dynamically to integrate local elements into a global percept.

papers.title: The role of hope and its association with quality of life in individuals with chronic pain - insights from a daily diary study.
papers.abstract: Hope has been identified as a beneficial factor for enhancing quality of life (QoL), particularly for individuals with chronic disease, including chronic pain. However, significant gaps remain in understanding how hope and QoL intersect and relate to one another. The current study investigated whether daily hope frequency, defined as how often participants felt hopeful each day, can predict next-day QoL among individuals with chronic pain who are using cannabis and opioids to manage pain. This was an observational study, approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health (Protocol: IRB00009327). Participants (N = 132) using opioids and cannabis for chronic pain completed a baseline survey and 30-day daily diaries assessing hope frequency, QoL, and sleep satisfaction. Participants (mean age = 42.7, SD = 13.9) were predominantly male (58.3%) and Non-Hispanic White (63.6%). Linear mixed-effects models were used to test the lagged effects of daily hope frequency, decomposed into between- and within-person components, on next-day QoL, controlling for baseline variables, daily sleep satisfaction, and previous-day QoL. Intraindividual variabilities were also examined. Higher hope frequency was significantly associated with greater next-day QoL both between participants (i.e., participants with higher average hope reported higher QoL) and within participants (i.e., on days when hope was higher than a participant's own average), even after controlling for previous-day QoL and sleep satisfaction. While higher baseline hope and QoL scores were associated with higher average QoL over the 30-day period, intraindividual variability in hope was not significantly associated with QoL. Our daily diary study found that previous-day hope frequency - both stable individual differences and day-to-day fluctuations - was associated with next-day QoL in individuals with chronic pain who were co-using cannabis and opioids.
papers.journal: Quality of life research : an international journal of quality of life aspects of treatment, care and rehabilitation

papers.title: Transcranial Evoked Potentials are Minimally Influenced by Afferent Feedback From Peripheral Muscle Contraction.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) investigates cortical reactivity, yet the contribution of sensory feedback from muscle twitches to the recorded signals remains debated. We combined M1 TMS-EEG with electromyography, accelerometry, and peripheral electrical stimulation to dissociate central and peripheral contributions. We compared EEG responses across trials yielding large versus small motor outputs, while peripheral stimulation isolated pure afferent components. Bayesian analysis revealed that larger motor outputs covaried with distinct EEG morphologies uniformly across all time windows-including those too early for peripheral feedback-indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in baseline motor cortex excitability drive both responses. Conversely, isolated muscle contraction produced delayed (> 65 ms), markedly smaller EEG responses with distinct spatiotemporal profiles. We conclude that sensory feedback from muscle twitches contributes minimally to TMS-evoked EEG responses, which instead primarily reflect the baseline excitability state of the stimulated cortex.

papers.title: [Orthognathic surgery for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea is a common, often serious breathing disorder characterised by repeated partial or complete obstruction of the upper airway during sleep. The diagnosis and treatment of this condition are complex and require collaboration between several specialists. The aetiology is multifactorial, with obesity, age, sex, smoking, alcohol and drug use, genetic factors, and anatomical abnormalities all playing an important role in the development of the condition. Morphological abnormalities of the jawbones are increasingly being recognised as a cause of respiratory disorders. Thus, the role of orthognathic surgery is becoming increasingly important in the treatment of certain types of obstructive sleep apnea. This paper describes the role of orthognathic surgery in treating obstructive sleep apnea, based on international literature and personal experience. It investigates the relationship between facial aesthetic abnormalities and sleep apnea, how craniofacial structure affects airway patency, the mechanisms by which jaw surgery can improve airway obstruction, the evidence supporting its effectiveness, and the factors that influence outcomes. The overarching aim of the current research is to determine in which cases of obstructive sleep apnea it is worthwhile to perform orthognathic surgery, either as a standalone treatment or as part of a combination therapy. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(43): 1730-1738.

papers.title: Mechanisms of auditory cortex injury and the protective effects of reoxygenation in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia.
papers.abstract: Intermittent hypoxia associated with obstructive sleep apnea can impair auditory function, but the early mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury and the extent to which these changes recover after the restoration of normoxia remain unclear. This study investigated the mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia and evaluated the protective effects of reoxygenation. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to control, intermittent hypoxia, intermittent hypoxia followed by 1 week of normoxic recovery, or control followed by normoxic recovery groups. Short-term intermittent hypoxia caused high-frequency hearing loss and increased spontaneous firing in the primary auditory cortex. After 1 week of normoxic recovery, auditory thresholds and cortical firing rates returned to levels comparable to those in the control group. Glutamate levels did not differ significantly among the groups, whereas γ-aminobutyric acid and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels were elevated in the intermittent hypoxia followed by normoxic recovery group. Intermittent hypoxia increased superoxide dismutase activity, reduced catalase activity, and elevated the levels of tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6. Normoxic recovery normalized catalase activity and reduced tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-6 levels, whereas superoxide dismutase activity and interleukin- 1β levels remained elevated. Metabolomic analysis identified alterations in unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, branched-chain amino acid metabolism, ferroptosis-related pathways, redox-related metabolism, and amino acid and protein turnover, several of which persisted after recovery. These findings indicate that acute intermittent hypoxia-induced auditory dysfunction and cortical hyperexcitability are reversible, whereas redox, inflammatory, and metabolic abnormalities recover asynchronously. Persistent molecular disturbances after functional recovery may provide potential targets for further investigation of obstructive sleep apnea-associated central auditory injury.

papers.title: High-dose cerium dioxide nanorods induce behavioral and electroencephalographic abnormalities through 5-HT1B receptor signaling disruption with an evaluation of anpirtoline's therapeutic potential.
papers.abstract: Cerium dioxide nanorods (CeO2 NRs) have drawn extensive research attention in the past few years for their exceptional generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and intrinsic catalytic properties. The two ends of the biological effect show a dose-dependent difference: protection of cells at low doses and damage to cells at high doses. Although the above processes are well documented in other biological contexts, the neurotoxicity induced by acute exposure to CeO2 NRs, as well as its mechanism and possible prevention strategies, have yet to be elucidated. In the present study, we have found that CeO2 NRs at a concentration of 500 μg/mL or higher induced neuronal apoptosis and reduced cell viability in vitro. After intranasal instillation in mice, CeO2 NRs accumulated in the lysosomes and nuclei of neurons in the hippocampus and striatum. There was an increase in these abnormal exploratory behaviors, heightened seizure susceptibility, and altered electroencephalographic (EEG) oscillations. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic profiling further indicated disruption of serotonin (5-HT) metabolism, caused by a downregulation of the 5-HT1B receptor, and thus provided a possible molecular mechanism for the behaviors and EEG abnormalities observed. Considerable changes also occurred in the various serotonergic mediators, neuronal excitability indicators, and inflammatory markers. Pharmacological activation of the 5-HT1B receptor with anpirtoline partially reversed the behaviors and EEG changes induced by CeO2 NRs.

papers.title: Phase-dependent EEG decoding of continuous visual stimuli.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations support cognition and perception by organizing information across oscillatory cycles. Although animal studies support this view, evidence in humans is mixed and largely based on transient stimuli. We tested whether alpha oscillations, the dominant human brain rhythm, periodically modulate the strength of visual representations. EEG was recorded while participants viewed long-lasting (2 s) Gabor patches. Using a phase-dependent decoding approach, we quantified stimulus decoding accuracy at specific alpha phases. Decoding performance varied systematically with alpha phase, following a smooth unimodal profile that peaked over occipito-parietal electrodes. These effects emerged well after stimulus onset and generalized to earlier time points, indicating a modulation of visual processing during continuous input. Our findings demonstrate that visual information is represented more accurately at specific alpha phases. This provides strong evidence that sensory processing is shaped by intrinsic brain dynamics and introduces a generalizable decoding pipeline for linking oscillatory phase to neural information processing.

papers.title: Aquatic Interventions for Children and Adolescents With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Motor, Sleep, Executive Function, and Adaptive Measures.
papers.abstract: Children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently face challenges in motor coordination, balance, sensory processing, sleep, physical activity engagement, and social and adaptive functioning. Aquatic interventions can offer a supportive therapeutic setting by combining physical activity, sensory input, motor practice, and opportunities for functional participation. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of structured aquatic interventions in children and adolescents with ASD on aquatic skills and water safety, sleep, social and adaptive outcomes, motor and balance performance, executive function, biomarkers, quality of life, and participation-related outcomes. A search was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, and PEDro for studies involving participants aged 0 to 18 years with ASD who underwent structured hydrotherapy, aquatic therapy, swimming-based therapy, or other water-based interventions. A narrative synthesis was carried out for all eligible studies, while random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for controlled studies reporting comparable outcomes. Nineteen studies, reporting ASD samples totaling 342 participants, were included, and seven of these contributed to the quantitative synthesis. Aquatic skills and water safety produced the most consistently favorable findings. Pooled estimates favored aquatic intervention for sleep (Hedges' g = 1.76, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.16 to 2.37), motor and balance outcomes (g = 1.49, 95% CI: 0.91 to 2.07), and executive function (g = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.35 to 1.46). Social and adaptive outcomes similarly favored aquatic intervention, though the pooled effect did not reach statistical significance (g = 0.38, 95% CI: -0.17 to 0.94). Since most domain-specific meta-analyses included only two studies, the pooled estimates should be viewed with caution. Overall, aquatic interventions appear to support water safety, motor and balance performance, sleep, and possibly executive function in pediatric ASD, while effects on social and adaptive functioning remain uncertain.

papers.title: Chronotherapy for retinopathy: Unraveling the mystery of Rev-erbα in the circadian rhythm.
papers.abstract: Disruption of the retinal circadian rhythm is a common manifestation of various retinal diseases, characterized by abnormal expression of clock genes and impaired light signaling in intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). This review aims to elucidate the mechanisms of circadian disruption in retinal pathologies, explore the interrelationship between clock genes and ipRGCs, and delineate the therapeutic potential and directions of chronotherapy for retinopathies. Through a systematic retrieval and analysis of literature on retinal diseases and circadian rhythms from databases including PubMed and Web of Science, this review reveals that Rev-erbα and melanopsin form an antagonistic system within the retina, regulating the intraocular dopamine-melatonin rhythm and maintaining retinal homeostasis. Disruption of this rhythmic system leads to oxidative stress, inflammation, and dysregulation of emotional responses. Moreover, chronotherapy, as an intervention leveraging intrinsic temporal patterns, holds significant promise for treating retinopathies associated with circadian misalignment.

papers.title: Circadian misalignment associates with inflammation, gut barrier, and microbiome composition in humans with obesity.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption has been linked to metabolic syndrome, but the biological links between circadian phenotypes and metabolic inflammation in humans remain incompletely characterized. We analyzed 87 adults with obesity from a randomized clinical trial to examine whether gut microbiome features and intestinal permeability relate to circadian misalignment and metabolic inflammation. Circadian phenotype was assessed using chronotype and meal timing, metabolic inflammation through a composite score of multiple biological measures, and gut permeability using sugar absorption testing. Late chronotype was associated with greater metabolic syndrome burden, while circadian misalignment was associated with increased gut permeability and inflammation, an association stronger among participants with higher permeability. These patterns co-occurred with lower abundance of short-chain fatty acid-associated bacteria, and intervention-related changes in permeability corresponded with changes in these taxa. These findings link circadian phenotypes with gut barrier and microbial features relevant to metabolic risk in obesity.

papers.title: Caring for the Caregivers: A Narrative Review of Physician Health Protection Across High-Income Countries and Lessons for Low- and Middle-Income Countries.
papers.abstract: Healthcare physicians (HCPs) across the world experience substantial mental, physical, and occupational health challenges, yet they remain an often-neglected group within healthcare systems. High levels of burnout, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, professional dissatisfaction, and even suicide have been reported in diverse settings, directly affecting patient safety and overall health system performance. This narrative review aimed to synthesize existing evidence on physician mental, physical, and professional health, with particular attention to similarities and differences between high-income countries (HICs) and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Peer-reviewed scientific articles, policy documents, and credible international reports examining physician well-being and workforce protection were analyzed. Recurrent themes across regions include burnout, depression, suicide risk, unsafe working conditions, professional dissatisfaction, migration, and collective actions such as strikes. In line with the objective of this review, the evidence also highlights important differences in how these challenges manifest and are addressed in HICs compared with LMICs. Although many of these problems are present globally, their severity is often greater in LMICs because of weaker occupational protections, limited access to mental health services, financial insecurity, and structural constraints within under-resourced health systems. The review therefore emphasizes that physician health should be viewed as a system-level and ethical responsibility rather than an individual failing. It further proposes practical and policy-oriented strategies that LMICs can adopt, such as confidential support pathways, regulatory reforms, and leadership accountability, to strengthen physician well-being without requiring major infrastructure expansion.

papers.title: Transient clinical improvement and immune modulation following recombinant Zoster vaccination in a patient with ME/CFS.
papers.abstract: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a debilitating multisystem disorder associated with immune dysregulation yet lacks definitive biomarkers or effective therapies. Acute immune perturbations may transiently modulate disease manifestations. We report the case of a female patient in her 60s with severe, long-standing ME/CFS who experienced changes in symptom following administration of recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV; Shingrix). Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were analyzed pre- and post-vaccination using flow cytometry, with comparison to a female healthy control. Plasma galectin-9 (Gal-9) levels were quantified by ELISA. Both RZV doses were associated with rapid, transient remission of symptoms, including improved sleep, cognition, pain, mobility, and respiratory function, followed by relapse. Immunologically, pre-vaccination profiling revealed elevated monocytes, increased CD71+ erythroid cells, and features of T cell exhaustion marked by Gal-9/PD-1 co-expression and impaired cytokine responses. Post-vaccination, monocyte frequency decreased, Gal-9+/PD-1+ T cells were reduced, and NK cell degranulation improved, indicating partial restoration of immune function. This case demonstrates that immune stimulation via RZV may transiently reverse immune dysfunction and improve clinical symptoms in ME/CFS. These findings support a role for reversible immune exhaustion in disease pathogenesis and highlight potential avenues for biomarker development and therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Integrated assessment of driving performance, eye movements, and cognitive function in obstructive sleep apnea: A pilot study.
papers.abstract: Motor vehicle accident (MVA) risk is greater in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet the functional domains most closely linked to driving-related impairment remain incompletely understood. This exploratory pilot study aimed to perform an integrated assessment of driving performance, eye movements, vigilance, and cognitive function in OSA and to examine their relationships with disease severity and treatment response. Adult drivers with suspected OSA underwent assessment using a driving simulator, Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), eye-tracking, and the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB). Participants with moderate-to-severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥20) who initiated continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy underwent re-evaluation after 6-12 months. At baseline, single-task reaction time in the driving simulator was positively correlated with apnea severity. In contrast, response accuracy under multitask plus steering conditions was associated with nocturnal hypoxemia (T90), suggesting differential contributions of apnea frequency and oxygen desaturation to driving performance. Eye-tracking parameters, including saccade amplitude and fixation duration, were significantly correlated with both driving performance and spatial working memory error scores. Following CPAP therapy, simple reaction times improved in both the driving simulator and PVT, whereas changes in multitasking performance and CANTAB measures were not statistically significant. Basic psychomotor speed was associated with OSA severity and improved following CPAP therapy, suggesting within-subject improvement of vigilance-dependent processes. In contrast, integrated oculomotor and executive function measures were more closely linked to complex driving performance, indicating that multidomain assessment may better characterize driving-related impairment in OSA. These findings provide preliminary evidence to guide future hypothesis-driven studies.

papers.title: Biological Mechanisms Underlying the Adverse Health Consequences of Human Circadian Misalignment from Night Shift Work.
papers.abstract: The waking and working times of night shift workers are displaced relative to the natural light/dark cycle, putting behavioral patterns in misalignment with the circadian regulation of biological processes. This state of circadian misalignment constitutes a circadian health problem, with widespread negative consequences for metabolic, cardiovascular, and mental health, as well as elevated risk of cancer. Scientific advances over the past decade have shed light on key aspects of the underlying biological mechanisms. With a focus on recent human studies, this paper reviews novel insights into what drives the adverse health consequences of circadian misalignment due to night shift work. Misalignment between the central circadian pacemaker and externally driven behavioral patterns during night shift work produces a rapid uncoupling of peripheral rhythms, reflected in the cargo of exosomes and other signaling mechanisms, and causes conflict between central and peripheral regulatory mechanisms. This endogenous internal desynchrony has been shown to be linked to shifted meal timing and, in part, may be mediated by the gut microbiome. Endogenous internal desynchrony leads to insulin resistance - a manifestation of metabolic dysfunction. It perturbs the cardiometabolic and immune systems, and also erodes mental health. At the cellular level, mistimed DNA repair mechanisms leave residual DNA damage after exposure to a night shift schedule - which, over time, may result in genomic instability and ultimately carcinogenesis. A systems biology perspective serves to elucidate how the effects of endogenous circadian disruption from night shift work increase the risk of acute and chronic illnesses. Internal desynchrony, endogenous in nature, is a common underlying cause. Time-restricted eating may help to address metabolic dysfunction due to night shift work; countermeasures for other negative health outcomes, including cancer and mental health disorders, remain to be developed.

papers.title: THE MYTH OF 98.6: A VITAL SIGN TAKEN FOR GRANTED.
papers.abstract: For over a century, 98.6°F/37°C has been commonly accepted as the benchmark for normal body temperature. In addition, 100.4°F/38°C has been the threshold for a fever. However, a growing body of evidence suggests these values are outdated and oversimplified. These values, derived in part, from Carl Wunderlich's nineteenth-century work, fail to account for modern data, circadian variation, and individual baseline differences. Contemporary studies reveal a lower average body temperature, and this suggests a need for redefining body temperature thresholds. Despite the clinical significance of this vital sign, it remains inconsistently defined across clinical guidelines. Recognizing abnormal body temperature as a spectrum rather than a fixed threshold may improve diagnostic accuracy and ultimately patient outcomes. This paper challenges the historical fixation surrounding 98.6°F/37°C and 100.4°F/38°C, calling for a modernized, context-driven approach to temperature interpretation.

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation.
papers.abstract: Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. Participants had a mean age of 73.8 ± 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome (β: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS (β: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: Cross-Band Coupling of EEG Infraslow Oscillations during NREM Sleep in Mice.
papers.abstract: The infraslow oscillation (ISO) is a ~ 0.02 Hz rhythmic fluctuation in electroencephalographic (EEG) power during NREM sleep. Prior studies were limited to sigma-band ISO, linked to rhythmic norepinephrine release in mice. Whether ISOs exist in other bands, and how ISOs across bands are coupled, remain unknown. We analyzed cross-band ISO coupling across six frequency bands during NREM using a wild-type (WT) discovery dataset of 122 recordings from 72 mice and WT validation of 7 mice. A transgenic (TG) validation of 6 mice was added to test ISO coupling's robustness to Cre knock-in on the LepR gene (LepR-Cre). Band power time series were filtered to the ISO range of 0.01-0.03 Hz. Cross-band coupling was assessed using Spearman's correlation and phase-locking value (PLV) across all 15 band pairs. ISOs were strongest in alpha, sigma, beta, and theta bands, weak in gamma, and absent in delta. Alpha, sigma, beta, and theta ISOs formed a highly correlated motif with replication in WT and TG (r = 0.61-0.77), while gamma had moderate correlation (r = 0.30-0.42), and delta was uncorrelated (p > 0.05). All band pairs showed significant phase locking with replication (FDR-corrected q < 0.01), with stronger consistency in alpha, sigma, theta, and beta (PLV 0.54-0.71), and weaker consistency involving delta and gamma (PLV 0.12-0.37). EEG ISOs extend beyond the sigma band to alpha, beta, and theta bands, forming a strongly coupled motif that may reflect a fundamental organization principle of sleep microstructures at a minute scale.

papers.title: Compensatory drive and sleep-related phantom limb pain: the moderating role of autonomic reserve.
papers.abstract: Phantom limb pain (PLP) is common after amputation, yet why poor sleep becomes pain in only some individuals is unknown. We hypothesized that a regulatory response is interpretable only against the reserve sustaining it, and thus we tested whether autonomic capacity relative to demand moderates the sleep-pain relationship in 121 amputee adults. Sleep was assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; PLP, residual limb pain (RLP), and phantom limb sensation (PLS) on 0-10 scales. Heart rate variability was summarized as autonomic reserve (log-transformed SDNN, RMSSD, total and high-frequency power) and autonomic drive (normalized low-frequency power). Poorer sleep was associated with greater PLP and RLP, but not PLS. No single HRV index moderated these associations, but the sleep × reserve × drive interaction did for PLP (b = -0.51, p = 0.026). Poor sleep predicted pain most strongly under high drive with reduced reserve. PLP vulnerability reflects autonomic capacity relative to demand, instead of any single HRV marker alone.

papers.title: Astrocytic timekeepers and their influence on brain waste clearance in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is associated with disruptions in circadian rhythmicity, yet the underlying mechanisms remain only partially understood. Developing insights suggest that astrocytes possess their own intrinsic circadian clocks, influencing multiple functions in brain homeostasis. Given the central role of astrocytes in brain waste clearance, this review investigates how the astrocytic clock mediates brain waste clearance and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology. By reviewing recent findings on extracellular clearance, cellular protein homeostasis, cellular detoxification/redox defence and neurotransmitter homeostasis, this review bridges research on astrocytic clock disruption with altered brain waste clearance dynamics. It further highlights the relevance of these alterations to Alzheimer's disease pathology. Interestingly, some clock-gene disruptions are associated with markers suggestive of increased autophagic activity and glymphatic-related gene expression, which may represent a compensatory response to circadian clock alteration. However, whether these changes translate into improved functional clearance in vivo, and whether they meaningfully affect Alzheimer's disease progression, remains uncertain. In contrast, similar clock-gene alterations generally impair blood-brain barrier integrity, glutamate clearance and antioxidant response, decreasing waste clearance capacity. These findings suggest a possible bidirectional relationship, in which some pathways may partially compensate for impairments in others. However, it remains unclear to what extent an imbalance in these pathways contributes to the development and/or progression of Alzheimer's disease. Altogether, the astrocytic circadian clock is positioned as an important regulator of brain waste clearance and warrants future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.

papers.title: REM sleep infraslow rhythms correlate with neuropsychiatric symptom severity.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is commonly divided into phasic and tonic substates based on higher and lower oculomotor activity, respectively. Our previous study described an alternative framework in which REM temporal structure forms a continuum of infraslow rhythms (∼0.01 Hz) across brain and body physiology. We now ask whether these infraslow rhythms vary with neuropsychiatric symptoms, given the long-standing but still inconsistent links between REM and mood- or trauma-related disorders. Using a cross-sectional polysomnographic dataset from male veterans, we examined 59 participants for correlations between REM infraslow rhythms and neuropsychiatric symptom scores, excluding participants with moderate/severe apnea. Oscillations in REM respiratory rate, but not cardiac rate or electroencephalogram beta power, showed higher infraslow frequencies in participants with multiple symptoms, including posttraumatic stress, pain, anxiety, depression, and cognitive difficulties. No significant correlations were found between these symptoms and conventional REM metrics (e.g., REM density, latency and duration). To further examine REM beyond phasic/tonic binarization, we analyzed the timing between oculomotor activity and infraslow oscillations. Eye movements occurred preferentially during periods of high respiratory rate, low beta power and intermediate cardiac rate, with no changes in these temporal relationships across symptom severity. Neuropsychiatric associations with REM infraslow rhythms spanned multiple symptom domains but were physiologically specific, with respiratory rate oscillations representing the strongest readout of symptom burden. Furthermore, REM infraslow cycles across brain and body were differentially aligned with eye movements: a temporal pattern that may serve as a physiological target for neuropsychiatric and mechanistic research. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep has long been studied in relation to neuropsychiatric conditions, but traditional measures of the timing and duration of REM episodes have shown limited consistency for symptom tracking. This study addresses this gap by highlighting a less explored physiological feature within REM episodes: minute-scale, or infraslow, rhythms in respiratory and cardiac rate, as well as oculomotor and brain activity. We report that REM infraslow oscillations, particularly in respiratory rate, occur at higher frequency in participants with worse trauma/mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties. This work is evidence of a possible new REM sleep-based biomarker for multiple diseases.

papers.title: Potential effect of replacing sedentary behavior with physical activity on the risk of atrial fibrillation: results from the UK Biobank and REGARDS study.
papers.abstract: Background Sedentary behavior (SB) has been associated with cardiovascular disease risk, independent of physical activity (PA) and sleep. However, the effect of replacing SB with PA or sleep on atrial fibrillation (AF) risk remains unclear. Methods We studied 86,096 participants from the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB) and 5,777 from the United States (US) REasons for Geographic And Racial Differences in Stroke (REGARDS) prospective cohort studies who were free of AF at baseline and had valid accelerometry data. The two cohorts were included to evaluate the consistency of associations across distinct populations in the UK and the US, two regions with a high burden of AF. Daily time spent in light PA (LPA), moderate to vigorous PA (MVPA), and SB were derived from accelerometer recordings; sleep was accelerometer-derived in UKB and self-reported in REGARDS. Incident AF was identified using ICD-10 codes (I48.x) listed as either a primary diagnosis, secondary diagnosis, or cause of death through hospital and death registry data linkage in UKB and in a follow-up visit through electrocardiogram and self-reported medical history in REGARDS. Isotemporal substitution models were used to examine replacing 30 minutes of SB with LPA or MVPA in both cohorts and with sleep in UKB on the outcome of incident AF. Results Among the UKB participants [57% female, mean age 56.0 (SD 7.8) years, 98% White race], 4,035 AF cases were identified during a median of 7.9 years of follow-up. Replacing 30 minutes of SB with PA was associated with a slightly lower risk of AF in the minimally adjusted models but the associations were attenuated after full adjustment (LPA: HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.02; MVPA: HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.02). The REGARDS participants had an average age of 63 (SD 8.3) years, 55% female, 31% Black and 69% White adults, with 486 AF cases identified. Fully adjusted substitution of 30 minutes of SB with MVPA was associated with lower AF odds (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.63-1.01), whereas LPA showed no association. In UKB, replacing SB with sleep was not associated with AF risk. The magnitude of the association of MVPA substitution with AF appeared stronger among REGARDS participants aged ≥65 years and those reporting <7 hours/day of sleep. Conclusion Replacing SB with moderate or higher intensity PA may decrease AF risk. In REGARDS, these substitutions appeared to benefit older individuals and those reporting shorter sleep duration. These findings highlight the potential benefit of reducing sedentarism to lower AF burden, warranting validation in future studies.

papers.title: [Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Interstitial Lung Disease: an underdiagnosed comorbidity].
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common yet underdiagnosed comorbidity that significantly affects the clinical course, quality of life, and prognosis of patients with interstitial lung disease (ILD). The interaction between these two conditions suggests the presence of bidirectional pathophysiological mechanisms. The diagnosis of OSA in this setting is challenging due to symptom overlap and the limitations of currently available screening tools. Regarding the management of OSA in patients with ILD, there are no randomized clinical trials evaluating the use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). This article reviews the available evidence on the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment of OSA in ILD.

papers.title: Vibrotactile transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) during working memory: convergent electrophysiological evidence for cortical efficiency.
papers.abstract: Working memory, the cognitive ability to maintain and manipulate a finite amount of information, is fundamental in reasoning, learning, and decision-making. Working memory erodes in conditions from Alzheimer's disease to stroke to healthy aging. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a promising neuromodulation method for improving working memory. By stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, taVNS is thought to engage ascending arousal systems such as the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system. However, the physiological link between LC-NE system modulation via taVNS and improved working memory remains largely unknown. This mechanistic gap limits the rational optimization of the stimulation protocol and the identification of the cognitive functions and patient populations that are likely to benefit. We test two competing hypotheses for how taVNS may improve working memory: sensory amplification or enhancement of cortical efficiency. The sensory-amplification hypothesis predicts increased cortical responses to stimuli, whereas the cortical-efficiency hypothesis predicts reduced cortical responses. Twenty healthy adults completed N-back working memory tasks during three counterbalanced sessions: baseline, active vibrotactile taVNS (vtaVNS), and sham stimulation, while we simultaneously recorded electroencephalography, electrocardiography, eye-tracking, and behavioral responses. To study the effect of vtaVNS on neuronal activity, we also recruited 20 patients with epilepsy undergoing invasive monitoring. Of these, 19 fully completed the spatial working-memory task. We quantified cortical responses to visual stimuli using event-related potentials (ERPs) in scalp EEG and high-gamma activity in intracranial local field potentials. To examine prediction of the cortical-efficiency hypothesis, we further explored the effect of vtaVNS on distance to criticality and heartbeat-evoked potentials. Active vtaVNS reduced both scalp-recorded visual ERP and high-gamma response in temporal cortices, relative to sham stimulation. Moreover, smaller visual event-related potentials were associated with successful encoding during the most demanding working-memory condition (i.e., 4-back task). Exploratory analyses showed that vtaVNS shifted cortical dynamics closer to criticality. Our results converge on the conclusion that vtaVNS does not uniformly amplify cortical responses to external stimuli. Instead, vtaVNS enhances cortical efficiency, supporting more effective allocation of cognitive resources between exteroceptive and mnemonic processes. These findings provide a framework for predicting when taVNS will be most beneficial and for optimizing stimulation protocols across cognitive and clinical applications. papers.title: Toward Reliable Patient-Specific Aortic Strain Mapping from 4D CTA: Validation, Spectral Structure, and Clinical Potential.
papers.abstract: To develop and validate a framework for spatially resolved ascending aortic strain estimation from 4D computed tomography angiography (CTA) and characterize reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales. We constructed patient-specific aortic strain maps using nnU-Net segmentation, optimized surface remeshing, deformable registration, and mesh-based strain estimation. Finite element (FE)-derived synthetic 4D CT sequences provided controlled reference deformations for registration validation. Strain reliability was characterized across segmentation sources and Laplace-Beltrami (LB) spectral scales. Associations with diameter, aortic height index (AHI), and age were assessed. Registration-derived median strain showed minimal bias relative to FE-reference strain for observer-derived (0.0013) and nnU-Net-derived meshes (0.0056). Median strain exhibited low bias and narrow 95% limits of agreement (LoA) across segmentation sources (interobserver: bias = -0.0045, LoA [-0.0490, 0.0399]; nnU-Net versus observer: bias = -0.0052, LoA [-0.0340, 0.0237]). Differences were greater for 95th-percentile strain, particularly in the interobserver comparison. LB spectral analysis showed preferential preservation of low-frequency strain organization, with k = 5 reconstructions reducing segmentation-related disagreement by 52-56%. The 95th-percentile areal strain was inversely associated with maximum ascending aortic diameter (r = -0.493, p = 0.005), AHI (r = -0.488, p = 0.005), and age (r = -0.479, p = 0.006). Three high-grade AR cases showed heterogeneous regional strain patterns. This framework reproducibly estimates ascending aortic strain from 4D CTA, characterizes its reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales, and demonstrates its potential for noninvasive assessment of patient-specific aortic mechanics.

papers.title: Sustained Viral Suppression and its association with Psychiatric Morbidity and Sleep Quality among Older Adults with Human Immunodeficiency Virus: Evidence from a Retrospective Cohort in Ibadan, Nigeria.
papers.abstract: Purpose Older adults with HIV are at risk of psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality, but evidence from sub-Saharan Africa is limited, particularly regarding sustained viral suppression. This study examined the prevalence of psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality symptoms and their association with sustained viral suppression among older adults with HIV in Nigeria. A retrospective cohort study was conducted among older adults receiving care at a tertiary HIV clinic in Ibadan, Nigeria. Viral load data from 2019-2023 were abstracted from medical records to determine sustained viral load suppression, while psychiatric morbidity and sleep quality were assessed cross-sectionally in 2023. Psychiatric assessments included major depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder and mania. Mixed-effects logistic regression assessed changes in viral suppression over time and associations with psychiatric morbidity and sleep quality. Among 400 participants, 63.5% were female and mean age was 58.2 years (S.D 6.5). A total of 25.8% had major depressive disorder, 17.5% had anxiety disorder, 29.3% had poor sleep quality, 3.3%, bipolar disorder, and 1.0% mania. Viral suppression improved significantly over the retrospective period. Sustained viral suppression was significantly associated with higher odds of good sleep quality (OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07 to 2.66, p = 0.025), but not psychiatric morbidity. Psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality are common among older adults with HIV in Nigeria. Sustained viral suppression was associated with better sleep quality but not psychiatric morbidity highlighting the importance of integrating mental health and sleep assessment into comprehensive HIV care for older adults.

papers.title: Activation pathway of the human voltage-gated proton channel.
papers.abstract: Many protein functions are coupled to proton transfer, yet the underlying mechanisms remain extremely difficult to resolve by experiment or conventional molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The human voltage-gated proton channel H V 1 (hH V 1) plays key roles in human physiology, but how voltage and pH together drive its activation remains unresolved. Experimental structures of hH V 1 are limited to the X-ray structure of a mouse chimera and NMR models of a truncated hH V 1, both representing an intermediate resting state. Here we determine the activation pathway of hH V 1, together with structural models of its resting and activated states, using an approach that integrates all-atom continuous constant-pH MD (CpHMD), weighted-ensemble (WE) path sampling, and AlphaFold modeling. Starting from an AlphaFold model selected for consistency with resting-state experimental data, over 100 µ s of simulations reveal a mechanism in which transmembrane voltage, assisted by proton titration, drives an outward displacement of the transmembrane segment S4 accompanied by a one-click reorganization of countercharge pairings. These events are enabled by a delicately balanced electrostatic landscape and pH-modulated breathing motions in the resting state that prime the channel for protonation-state switches upon voltage sensing, a principle that may underlie other proton-coupled voltage-gating processes. The simulations also uncover lipid-binding sites at which POPG selectively stabilizes the S4-up conformation, whereas POPE can stabilize either state. These predictions are validated against extensive electrophysiology, mutagenesis data, and new smFRET experiments, which support the one-click S4 displacement and the lipid effects. WE-CpHMD, implemented in the AMBER package, is applicable to other proton-coupled processes that remain elusive.

papers.title: Asymmetric assembly underlies activation mechanism of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels.
papers.abstract: G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK; Kir3) channels are principal effectors of inhibitory GPCR signaling. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule imaging, electrophysiology and molecular dynamics to define the architecture and activation of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels. GIRK1/2 preferentially assembles as an asymmetric heterotetramer containing one GIRK1 and three GIRK2 subunits. Three PIP₂ molecules bound to GIRK2 promote partial cytoplasmic-domain docking, whereas engagement of a fourth PIP₂ by GIRK1 completes docking and opens the helix bundle crossing gate. GIRK1 also remodels the electrostatic environment beneath the selectivity filter, where its E141 and D173 residues create a permeation module that enhances K⁺ conduction. The GIRK1-selective activator ML297 binds at the GIRK1-GIRK2 interface and controls both permeation and gating. These findings establish how asymmetric assembly couples sequential lipid-dependent gating to efficient K⁺ permeation and GIRK1-dependent pharmacological activation.
